evidence: The number of Chinese English-language journals (celajs) has increased from 83 in 1980 to over 500 today, with a commensurate increase in the number of university presses and over 8000 journals. Large scholarly publishers such as China Science Publishing Group Co., Ltd (CSPG) and Social Sciences Academic Press (SSAP) of the Chinese Association of Social Science (CASS), account for much of this growth.

unit: China's higher education and education system expanded dramatically: annual graduates rose from 0.87 million in 1999 to over 8.7 million, public education investment rose from 2.7% to 4.1% of GDP between 1992 and 2018, and college admissions rose from 3.7 million in 2000 to 9.1 million in 2019.
evidence: China now graduates more than 8.7 million students each year (a ten-fold increase from the 0.87 million graduates in 1999). Public investment in Chinese education soared 50-fold between 1992 and 2018, from 2.7% of the GDP to 4.1%.

unit: China's ambivalence toward market-led neoliberal development under the Washington Consensus, along with the state's capacity to marshal its large population, is credited with enabling it to catch up to advanced economies.
evidence: While China's focus on labor-intensive industries has followed other Asian economies, the country's ambivalence toward neoliberal (market-led) development prescribed by the Washington Consensus has enabled it to catch up to advanced economies, even as the vast majority of developing countries have made little progress.

unit: China treats human capital development as a prominent feature of national policy to reduce technological dependence on the US and other advanced economies, and its 5G and AI-mediated techno-state may make its development model a global standard.
evidence: In its drive to reduce its technological dependence on the United States and other advanced economies, Chinese human capital development is becoming a prominent feature of national policy and planning.

unit: The US Trade Representative identifies elements of China's development approach as central planning, mobilization across sectors, state resources and finance, civil-military integration, backbone technology enterprises, breakthroughs in key areas, import substitution, and promotion of domestic industries.
evidence: The Office of the United States Trade Representative notes the elements of China's development approach includes central planning, plan mobilization across all sectors, the leveraging of state resources and finance, civilmilitary integration and two-way transfer, backbone enterprises in technology development, technological breakthroughs in key areas, import substitution policies, and the promotion of Chinese industries in its domestic market.

unit: The expansion of China's Belt and Road Initiative across emerging economies, built on global interconnectivity and research collaboration among higher education institutions, represents a new Chinese-led development model.
evidence: Building on investments in global interconnectivity and overlapping research collaboration across HE institutions, the expansion of China's BRI across emerging economies represents a new Chinese-led development model.

unit: Chinese infrastructuralism is a State-led development model, distinct from US-led neoliberal trade liberalization, in which education is critical; it is proposed as a new stage in globalization and a new development model.
evidence: Unlike US-led trade liberalization (neoliberalism), education is critical to what might be called "Chinese infrastructuralism". Chinese infrastructuralism represents a new stage in globalization and a new model of development.

unit: Chinese infrastructuralism layers infrastructure investment, combining physical infrastructure such as ports and railways with people-to-people exchanges, the digital Silk Road, university alliances and educational and cultural exchanges, i.e. both hard and soft infrastructure for developing skilled labor.
evidence: Following the Chinese model, infrastructure investment and development is layered, including not only physical infrastructure such as the development of transport networks (ports and railways) but also people-to-people exchanges emphasizing the new digital Silk Road, university alliances and the development of educational and cultural exchanges.

unit: The Belt and Road Initiative began as a large infrastructure project but has expanded to include culture and education as the soft infrastructure of a regional trading system, with potential to reshape higher and vocational education across Eurasia.
evidence: What began as an enormous infrastructure project has evolved to include a new series of goals overlapping culture and education-in the broadest sense, to form the "soft infrastructure" of a massive regional trading system. BRI represents a pillar of the "Chinese Dream", providing a new model of development with the potential to reshape both higher and vocational education across the Eurasian region (Peters, 2020).

unit: The Chinese government links study in China to job opportunities across BRI countries, even as many Western universities expect declining student enrolment.
evidence: Even as many universities across Western countries expect declining student enrolment (Redden, 2019), the Chinese government has linked study in China to job opportunities across BRI countries.

unit: As Chinese higher education improves in quality and capacity and is combined with scholarships and a large economy, China's impact on global higher education could be very large, with Chinese universities absorbing students worldwide.
evidence: Combined with generous scholarship programs and an enormous economy, China's impact on global HE could be enormous. Indeed, as the quality and capacity of Chinese HE continue to improve, Chinese universities will continue to absorb eager students from around the world.

unit: Rising demand for STEM education and China's drive to reduce technological dependence are expected to increase China's attractiveness as a study destination and expand its STEM education capacity, affecting the global higher education market.
evidence: As demand for education continues to increase, particularly across STEM subjects, China's attractiveness as a study destination for emerging economies will grow, impacting the global HE market more broadly. As China seeks to reduce its technological dependence on others, its capacities for supporting STEM education can be expected to grow in scale and quality.

unit: Future BRI investments built on Chinese AI and next-generation technologies could enable digital convergence and accelerate globalization toward a multipolar system.
evidence: Rooted in next-generation technologies such as AI, deep learning, smart cities, quantum computing, and the Internet-of-Things, Chinese trade and investments could enable the vast digital convergence and economic synergies that many have been theorizing over the past decade (Peters, 2012).

unit: China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) is a uniquely Chinese approach to development, involving over 149 countries and more than a trillion dollars of planned investment in economic, digital and social development across multiple continents.
evidence: With over 149 countries involved in China's Belt and Road system and over a trillion dollars of Chinese investment planned for economic, digital and social development across multiple continents, BRI represents a uniquely Chinese approach to development.

unit: Belt and Road regions could contribute as much as 80% of global GDP growth by 2050 and move three billion more people into the middle class.
evidence: Belt and Road regions could contribute as much as 80% of global GDP growth by 2050, advancing three billion more people into the middle class.

unit: BRI is more than an infrastructure project: it reflects a new stage of globalization in which multiple regions converge around Chinese-led globalization.
evidence: More than simply a global infrastructure project, BRI reflects a new stage in globalization in which multiple regions and geographies are now converging around a new era in Chinese-led globalization.

unit: China's large soft infrastructure of education and training could reconfigure the global higher education sector, much as China became the manufacturing workshop of the world.
evidence: Much as China has become the manufacturing workshop of the world, the country's enormous soft infrastructure of education and training could be set to reconfigure the global HE sector as well.

unit: Chinese foreign direct investment is underwriting a new multipolar order in which Chinese higher education could be key to global integration across emerging and developing countries.
evidence: What this suggests is that Chinese FDI is now underwriting a new multipolar order in which Chinese HE could be key to global integration across emerging and developing countries.

unit: Conclusions about BRI's final impact are premature because the initiative is still in an early phase of development, though preliminary trends in higher education's trajectory can be identified.
evidence: However, drawing far-reaching conclusions on the final impact of BRI may be premature. BRI is still in an early phase of development.

unit: Chinese telecom providers now dominate Africa's billion-user mobile phone market, as Chinese conglomerates position themselves to capitalize on the continent's need for technology, trade and manufacturing.
evidence: In Africa, for example, Chinese conglomerates have already become positioned to capitalize on the continent's need for technology, trade, and manufacturing. China's investments encompass utilities, port construction and agriculture but also telecommunications. Chinese telecom providers now dominate Africa's billion-user mobile phone market.

unit: China's strategy targeted 40% self-sufficiency by 2020 and 75% by 2025, encouraging STEM development in key digital technologies such as quantum computing, supercomputing, machine learning and genomic science.
evidence: On the basis of this strategy China aimed for 40% self-sufficiency by 2020 and 75% self-sufficiency by 2025 (Peters, 2019).These strategies have included the encouragement of development in STEM disciplines with a focus on key digital technologies in quantum computing (QC), supercomputing (SC), machine learning (ML), genomic science (GS), new materials science (NMS) and so on with the development the new range of strategic biodigital technologies that drives technological convergence focused on the emerging global digital economy and fintech.

unit: The number of domestic-born students in US AI doctorate programs has not grown since 1990, while competition for international students has intensified, threatening the US ability to retain international students and its lead in AI talent.
evidence: The number of domestic-born students participating in AI doctorate programs has not increased since 1990, and competition for international students has accelerated, endangering the United States' ability to retain international students (Zwetsloot et al., 2019).

unit: The only two ways for the United States to sustain its AI lead are to cultivate more talent at home and to recruit and retain more talent from foreign countries.
evidence: Cultivating more potential talent at home and recruiting and retaining more existing talent from foreign countries are the only two options to sustain the US lead.

unit: Between 2000 and 2014 China increased its STEM graduates by 360% (1.7 million in 2014), compared with a 54% rise in the United States, many of whom were international students.
evidence: Between 2000 and 2014, China's university system increased its number of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) graduates by 360%, producing 1.7 million in 2014 alone (The Rise of China, 2018). 2 The number of STEM graduates in the United States' university system rose by 54% during the same time period, and many were international students (Science & Engineering Indicators, 2018).

unit: China's researchers make up roughly 29% of the world's top-tier deep learning talent, and China and other states use flexible immigration policies and incentives to attract international tech talent.
evidence: China's researchers now represent roughly 29% of top-tier deep learning talent in the world (The Global AI Talent Tracker, 2020). 3 China and other states have also taken steps to attract international talent with flexible immigration policies and incentives for tech talent (Staff Report, 2019).

unit: The United States should invest in all AI talent pipelines, because a passive strategy will not work in the AI talent competition.
evidence: The United States needs to invest in all AI talent pipelines in order to remain at the forefront of AI now and into the future. A passive strategy will not work in the face of the AI talent competition.

unit: The Commission proposes that the United States train four archetypes of AI talent: researchers, implementers, end users, and informed consumers.
evidence: To achieve dominance in AI, the United States needs to train four archetypes to propel AI in America: Researchers, implementers, end users, and informed consumers.

unit: Researchers are AI research engineers and algorithm experts who focus on R&D of semi- and fully autonomous systems and drive development cycles from research to prototype testing.
evidence: Researchers: AI research engineers will focus on R&D of technologies that enable and advance semi- and fully autonomous systems. They serve as algorithm experts with up-to-date knowledge of modern AI research and may be involved in the inception of ideas and drive the development cycles from research to testing prototypes for a major project or component of a major project.

unit: Implementers handle data cleaning, feature selection, model training and tuning, and partnering with domain experts, and need roughly associate or bachelor's-level training that includes ethics and bias mitigation.
evidence: Developers require less training and education than AI experts, and will have training, education, and/or experience that is roughly equivalent to an associate or bachelor's degree; and that includes relevant ethics and bias mitigation in data processing and model training.

unit: Investing in STEM education alone will not be enough for the United States to win the international competition for AI and STEM talent, because its STEM education system lacks the capacity and quality to supply enough talent for its markets and national security enterprise.
evidence: Investments in STEM education alone, however, will not be enough for the United States to win the international competition for AI and STEM talent. China is producing large numbers of computer scientists, engineers, and other STEM graduates (The Rise of China, 2018). For the foreseeable future, the United States' STEM education system does not have the capacity nor the quality to produce sufficient STEM or AI talent to supply the United States' markets or national security enterprise.
section_path: The Promise and Limits of Expanding STEM

unit: The 1958 National Defense Education Act, passed after Sputnik, funded student loans, education at all levels and graduate fellowships, and enabled many more students to attend college; US college enrollment rose from 3.6 million in 1960 to 7.5 million in 1970.
evidence: The NDEA promoted the importance of science, mathematics, and foreign languages for students, authorizing more than $1 billion toward decreasing student loans, funding education at all levels, and funding graduate fellowships. Many students were able to attend college because of this legislation. In 1960, 3.6 million students attended college; by 1970 it was 7.5 million (Sputnik, 2020).
section_path: The Promise and Limits of Expanding STEM

unit: The Commission recommends a second National Defense Education Act (NDEA II) that funds digital skills such as mathematics, computer science, data science and statistics, covers K-12 education and reskilling, and targets under-resourced school districts.
evidence: NDEA II would focus on funding students acquiring digital skills, like mathematics, computer science, information science, data science, and statistics. NDEA II should include K-12 education and reskilling programs that address deficiencies across the spectrum of the American educational system, purposefully targeting under-resourced school districts.
section_path: The Promise and Limits of Expanding STEM

unit: The Commission recommends university-level STEM investments of 25,000 undergraduate, 5,000 graduate, and 500 PhD scholarships, with undergraduate awards including community college credit hours to make STEM education affordable and widen the digital talent pool for underrepresented Americans.
evidence: The Commission also recommends investments in university-level STEM programs with 25,000 undergraduate, 5,000 graduate, and 500 PhDlevel scholarships. Undergraduate scholarships should include credit hours at community colleges to ensure more Americans have access to affordable STEM education.
section_path: The Promise and Limits of Expanding STEM

unit: Highly skilled immigration is a national security imperative because nations that attract and retain skilled people gain strategic and economic advantages, especially in AI where talent demand far exceeds supply.
evidence: Immigration reform is a national security imperative. Nations that can successfully attract and retain highly skilled individuals gain strategic and economic advantages over competitors. Human capital advantages are particularly significant in the field of AI, where demand for talent far exceeds supply (Zwetsloot et al., 2019).
section_path: The Promise and Limits of Expanding STEM

unit: The United States benefits more from skilled immigration than other countries: in 2013 it had 15 times as many immigrant inventors as American inventors abroad, while Canada, Germany and the UK have net negative inventor immigration rates.
evidence: In 2013, the United States had 15 times as many immigrant inventors as there were American inventors living abroad (Fink, 2013). By contrast, Canada, Germany, and the United Kingdom. all maintain a net negative inventor immigration rate (Miguelez and Fink, 2013).
section_path: The Promise and Limits of Expanding STEM

unit: International students are increasingly studying elsewhere or returning home, partly due to the growing green card backlog, which forces many Indian immigrants to wait decades on restrictive work visas and hinders tech recruitment.
evidence: Unfortunately, international students in the United States are increasingly choosing to study in other countries or return home (Zwetsloot et al., 2019). 8 One reason is the growing backlog of green card petitions (Kahn and MacGarvie, 2020). Indian immigrants face a particularly long wait.
section_path: The Promise and Limits of Expanding STEM

unit: Curriculum Design and Renewal is an ongoing, cyclical, analytical process that continually seeks new and effective ways to give students transformational, inspiring and intellectually challenging learning experiences, and it centers on developing learning outcomes and choosing instruction methods.
evidence: Curriculum Design and Renewal refers to the "ongoing, cyclical, and analytical process, that continually strives to find new and effective ways to offer students learning experiences that are transformational, inspiring, and intellectually challenging" (Queens University 2019) and focuses on the identification and further development of learning outcomes and the choice of appropriate instruction methods.
section_path: 15.2 Cooperation between HEIs and Companies in Work-Based Higher Education

unit: DHBW builds industry involvement into its governance structure: rules agreed with the State of Baden-Wuerttemberg require industry representatives throughout administration and governance, so 50% of the managing board and senate members have an industry background and eight of 17 supervisory board members come from the private sector.
evidence: A comprehensive set of codes and rules, agreed upon both by the university as well as the State of Baden-Wuerttemberg, thus foresee that industry representatives be integrated throughout the university's administration and governance structure. As a consequence, 50% of the members of the managing board and the senate at DHBW have an industry background, and eight of the 17 members of the supervisory board come from the private sector (DHBW 2019).
section_path: 15.2 Cooperation between HEIs and Companies in Work-Based Higher Education

unit: At DHBW, practitioners advising on curriculum are asked to represent the general direction and needs of their whole industry rather than one company, and the senior, broadly experienced figures involved support this.
evidence: In this context, it is important to note that all practitioners are asked not to speak exclusively to the interests of a specific company, but to provide recommendations based on the general direction and needs of "their" industry overall. This idea is supported by the fact that many of the industry representatives who are involved in curriculum- or governance-related decisions at DHBW tend to be rather senior figures in their respective organizations with broad expertise and knowledge.
section_path: 15.2 Cooperation between HEIs and Companies in Work-Based Higher Education

unit: WIT brings in practical expertise through an all-industry Board of Trustees, Industry Advisory Committees, 30-50 University Advisers, and faculty members' personal connections.
evidence: Its governing body, the Board of Trustees, 22 for instance, is comprised exclusively of industry representatives, many of whom are also WIT alumni. Moreover, Industry Advisory Committees discuss a wide range of issues, including the performance and potential need for reform of specific programs 23 and there are 30-50 University Advisers who provide additional insights to the administration and trustees on issues of strategic importance.
section_path: 15.2 Cooperation between HEIs and Companies in Work-Based Higher Education

unit: WIT lacks mechanisms ensuring industry representatives promote industry-wide rather than single-firm needs, because its practitioners tend to be technical experts focused on their firm's immediate needs and US business is highly individualistic with no tradition of sectorial bargaining.
evidence: Yet, unlike DHBW, WIT does not have in place mechanisms to ensure that industry representatives promote learning content that represents the needs of an entire industry rather than a specific company. 25 This can be attributed to at least two factors: first, practitioners involved at WIT tend to be technical experts rather than senior managers, and therefore are most familiar with and focused on meeting their firm's immediate needs.
section_path: 15.2 Cooperation between HEIs and Companies in Work-Based Higher Education

unit: Because faculty want broad curricula while practitioners focus on specific firms' needs, WIT has fewer incentives than DHBW for joint course development, so industry input is limited to specific points such as guest lectures in its AI-in-architecture module.
evidence: Given the potential for conflict between academic faculty, who wish to keep the curriculum broad and general enough to meet the demands of a wider range of firms, and practitioners, focused on the needs of specific firms, incentives for the joint development of courses are thus more limited at WIT than at DHBW.
section_path: 15.2 Cooperation between HEIs and Companies in Work-Based Higher Education

unit: The authors recommend promoting the transparency, visibility, and accessibility of work-based higher education (WBHE) programs in the United States, supported by widely communicated quality standards and new funding models.
evidence: Going forward, we thus recommend that efforts be made to promote transparency, visibility, and accessibility of WBHE programs in the United States. Widely communicated quality standards and new funding models could help this cause.
section_path: 15.3 On the Potential of WBHE to Train the "Work of the Future"

unit: The German WBHE system could benefit from giving higher education institutions a greater ability to distinguish themselves from one another and to demonstrate their innovative potential.
evidence: The German system, by contrast, could benefit from a greater ability for HEI to distinguish themselves from others and demonstrate their innovative potential.
section_path: 15.3 On the Potential of WBHE to Train the "Work of the Future"

unit: In both the US and Germany, WBHE should put more emphasis on upskilling and retraining the existing workforce through continuing education, because the workforce of the future includes many talented people who have yet to learn to engage productively with new technologies, especially AI.
evidence: In both countries, WBHE should put a greater emphasis on enabling upskilling and retraining the existing workforce through continuing education. After all, the "workforce of the future" consists not only of tomorrow's students, but also of the large number of talented individuals who have yet to learn how to productively engage with new technologies and AI in particular.
section_path: 15.3 On the Potential of WBHE to Train the "Work of the Future"

unit: Bureau of Labor Statistics data show a skills mismatch: only 43% of US workers are trained for the 53% of US jobs that are middle skill.
evidence: Analyses of data by the Bureau of Labor Statistics has found that only 43% of US workers are trained for the 53% of US jobs that are middle skill (National Skills Coalition 2017).
section_path: 15.3 On the Potential of WBHE to Train the "Work of the Future"

unit: Work-based learning programs in the US often share a name but differ in value across institutions, depending on how well curricula align with regional labor market demand and on program quality.
evidence: With a view of work-based learning, Carnevale et al. underline that "programs are often the same in name only" and "have different values at different institutions depending on the alignment between particular curricula and regional labor market demand, as well as on differences in program quality" (2015, p. 18).
section_path: 15.3 On the Potential of WBHE to Train the "Work of the Future"

unit: Community colleges are often known for high dropout rates and associate's degrees rather than for their services, which gives them a reputation as inferior institutions.
evidence: Rather than for the important services they provide to many Americans, CCs are often known for their comparatively high dropout rates. As many of their graduates furthermore obtain an associate's rather than a bachelor's degree, community colleges have the reputation as being institutions of inferior quality.
section_path: 15.3 On the Potential of WBHE to Train the "Work of the Future"

unit: The Instruction and Training dimension of work-based higher education (WBHE) programs concerns how didactical knowledge and subject expertise are combined, through selecting instructors with practical expertise and organizing theory-focused and practice-oriented learning phases.
evidence: The Instruction and Training dimension of WBHE programs focuses on how didactical knowledge and subject-level expertise are combined through the careful selection and integration of instructors with practical expertise and the organization of theory-focused and practice-oriented learning phases.
section_path: 15.2 Cooperation between HEIs and Companies in Work-Based Higher Education

unit: In the United States, co-op programs are anchored only in a university's general accreditation guidelines, so the university decides independently whether and how far to rely on external partners for curriculum feedback or content. Germany's more extensively regulated structure therefore produces closer and more systematic integration of theory and practice.
evidence: In the United States, by contrast, the absence of a comparably extensively regulated structure means that co-op programs are anchored solely within the general accreditation guidelines of the university. This allows the university to determine independently whether and to which extent it wants to rely on external partners to provide feedback on or determine the contents of the curriculum. This leads to closer and more systematic integration of theory and practice in the German context than in the United States.
section_path: 15.2 Cooperation between HEIs and Companies in Work-Based Higher Education

unit: At DHBW only about 40% of courses are taught by full-time academics, and most teaching staff are experts employed by partner companies or social institutions. This favors instruction built on real-world examples and case studies over abstract theory, as seen in its AI analytics program.
evidence: The effect is further enhanced by the fact that at DHBW, only about 40% of courses are taught by the full-time academics of DHBW or partner universities. While these professors also tend to have a lot of industry experience, 30 most teaching staff are experts, employed mainly by partner companies or social institutions. This has implications for the teaching and instruction methods as it favors instruction with a strong reliance on real-world examples and case studies rather than abstract knowledge or theory.
section_path: 15.2 Cooperation between HEIs and Companies in Work-Based Higher Education

unit: DHBW's Blockmodell alternates practical and theoretical phases in a clearly defined three-month rhythm and governs about 80% of dual study programs in Germany. It is seen as particularly effective at linking theoretical knowledge with practical skills and lets students experience both university and company settings.
evidence: Furthermore, following a clearly defined three-month rhythm, DHBW's Blockmodell (block model), which governs approximately 80% of all dual study programs in Germany, is perceived to be particularly effective at promoting a direct link between theoretical knowledge and practical skills.
section_path: 15.2 Cooperation between HEIs and Companies in Work-Based Higher Education

unit: At WIT, students are mostly taught by full-time academic faculty, and industry background is not a formal requirement; hiring focuses on teaching ability, research quality, publications, and academic record.
evidence: At WIT, by contrast, students are mostly instructed by full-time academic faculty. While the latter can also have a background in industry, the latter is not a formal requirement.
section_path: 15.2 Cooperation between HEIs and Companies in Work-Based Higher Education

unit: WIT students complete only two mandatory co-op phases, in spring of year 3 and fall of year 4, so instruction has a strong academic bias. A third summer co-op after sophomore year is optional and does not count toward graduation.
evidence: Generally participating in only two (mandatory) co-op phases during the spring of the 3rd year and the fall of the 4th year respectively, students face instruction with a strong academic bias.
section_path: 15.2 Cooperation between HEIs and Companies in Work-Based Higher Education

unit: To ensure work-integrated education, WIT faculty use hands-on projects, lab sessions, and workshops throughout the semester, especially in new AI offerings where tools and real-world applications are considered highly beneficial.
evidence: To ensure high levels of work-integrated education, WIT faculty rely on hands-on projects, lab sessions, and workshops throughout the semester. This applies in particular to the newly developed educational offerings in the case of AI, where tools and real-world applications are considered highly beneficial.
section_path: 15.2 Cooperation between HEIs and Companies in Work-Based Higher Education

unit: The pandemic compressed nearly a decade of change in user behavior and technology preference into a few months, but the underlying advances had been developing for decades and key technologies were already widespread when lockdowns began.
evidence: The pandemic brought nearly a decade of change in user behavior and preference for technology in just a matter of months. While it may have served as the ultimate catalyst, these exponential advances have in fact been brewing for decades. The lockdowns began at a moment when many key technologies had already reached a point of widespread proliferation.

unit: India Stack is the name for India's public-private open-source platforms, begun after the 2009 Aadhaar launch, comprising interconnected systems for identity, payments, documents, and digitally signed transactions that accelerated digital adoption.
evidence: These ground-breaking public-private efforts have come to be known as "India Stack". It has comprised a series of interconnected systems for identity, payments, documents, and digitally signed transactions which have supercharged digital adoption throughout the country (India Stack, n.d.).

unit: Cheap, powerful AI, machine learning, and cloud computing from providers like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft enable scalable, distributed, individualized instruction tailored to specific needs.
evidence: Artificial intelligence, machine learning, and cloud computing are now abundantly accessible through services offered by companies like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft. This enables the processing possible for scale, distribution, and complex individualized instruction tailored to specific needs.

unit: Social media lets education companies market more cheaply and with better targeting, reaching new customers and delivering content in new languages, formats, and form factors to diverse audiences.
evidence: Social media has made marketing far cheaper and more targeted for education companies. This allows them to reach customers they could not previously access and deliver content in form factors, languages, and formats that were never before possible, to diverse audiences across the country.

unit: Despite progress in connectivity, access in India is uneven: only 11% of households have computers, and 54% of urban residents had internet access versus 32% of rural residents.
evidence: For all the progress the country has made in connectivity, gains have been unevenly distributed across the country's regions, populations, and income groups. According to an analysis by two major firms (Nielsen, 2014), only 11% of Indian households have computers such as desktops, laptops, and tablets. For the vast majority of the population, content consumption takes place on mobile devices. While 54% of urban residents reported having internet access, that was only true for 32% of rural residents.

unit: An Azim Premji University survey across five states found almost 60% of students could not properly access online learning, due to lacking smartphones, shared devices, software problems, or other issues.
evidence: One survey by Azim Premji University found that across five states, almost 60% of students surveyed could not properly access online learning opportunities. That was due to the absence of a smartphone, multiple users sharing one device, problems with the software, or other issues (Azim Premji University, 2020).

unit: Digital learning barriers in India disproportionately affect poor students and those with disabilities, and under these constraints teachers struggled to provide emotional connection, assessment, and attention.
evidence: Data suggests that barriers to participating effectively in digital learning remains a challenge for large portions of India's students, especially those who are poor or have disabilities.

unit: A survey by Azim Premji University across five Indian states found that almost 60% of students could not properly access online learning, due to lacking a smartphone, sharing one device among several users, software problems, or other issues.
evidence: One survey by Azim Premji University found that across five states, almost 60% of students surveyed could not properly access online learning opportunities. That was due to the absence of a smartphone, multiple users sharing one device, problems with the software, or other issues (Azim Premji University, 2020).

unit: Under pandemic-era constraints on remote learning, teachers in India reported struggling to provide the emotional connection, assessment, and attention needed for adequate instruction.
evidence: Additionally, with these constraints, teachers reported finding themselves struggling to provide the emotional connection, assessment, and attention needed for adequate instruction.

unit: In response to remote learning barriers, India saw a surge of public and informal supports, including textbooks, home visits, mass-communication tools, midday meals, sanitation kits, and monetary support, plus a government repository of curriculum and tools.
evidence: These include using traditional tools such as textbooks, home visits and mass-communication tools, in addition to learningenabling solutions such as midday meals, sanitation kits, and monetary support. The government's Ministry of Education made a large repository of learning curriculum and tools available while creating platforms for information sharing (UNICEF, 2021).

unit: India was a market ripe for digital learning because the pandemic worsened existing education and socioeconomic problems while simultaneously creating an unprecedented need for digital learning solutions.
evidence: The pandemic served to exacerbate many of the existing issues in India's education system and social-economic structures-creating both difficult conditions and an unprecedented need for digital learning solutions at the same time. If there was a market ripe for a digital learning transformation, it was India.

unit: Several Indian cultural and economic factors favored Edtech growth: strong emphasis on education and parental willingness to spend on it, education seen as the route to mobility, dissatisfaction with existing systems, and increasingly accessible cheap technology.
evidence: In the Indian cultural context, there is a large focus on education-and therefore parents are comparatively more willing to spend their disposable income on services for their children. As a developing nation, education is still seen as the most promising route to mobility. There is also widespread dissatisfaction with the status quo of most of the country's educational systems, so the existing options are insufficient. At the same time, Indian consumers have more practical access to cheap technology than ever before (Deloitte India, 2022).

unit: CB Insights identified 14 categories of Edtech product development, including online learning, learning management systems, career development, language learning, learning analytics and test prep; in India the largest gains were in test prep, offline tutoring, and career development.
evidence: But the largest gains have been made in the fields of test prep, offline tutoring, and career development (Inc 42, 2021).

unit: In 2020 over 15% of the more than $10B raised by Indian startups went to Edtech companies, and the amount more than doubled in 2021 to $4.7 billion.
evidence: In 2020, of the more than $10B raised by Indian startups, over 15% went to Edtech companies (Press Trust of India, 2021). The following year, in 2021, this more than doubled to $4.7 billion (Vanamali, 2022).

unit: The rapid expansion of AI has greatly benefited the education sector but also brings several ethical dilemmas.
evidence: In recent years, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has witnessed remarkable expansion, greatly benefiting the education sector. Nonetheless, this advancement brings forth several ethical dilemmas.

unit: Research on ethical concerns of AI in education is notably scarce, particularly research that takes the user's standpoint.
evidence: The existing research on these ethical concerns within the educational framework is notably scarce, particularly when viewed from a user's standpoint.

unit: A systematic review of 17 empirical articles found that the ethics of learning analytics and the ethics of algorithms in AIED are often neglected in existing ethical frameworks, principles, and standards for AIED.
evidence: The finding revealed that certain ethical aspects, including the ethics of learning analytics and the ethics of algorithms in AIED, are often neglected in the existing ethical frameworks, principles, and standards for AIED.

unit: Because of the gap between existing ethical frameworks and users' ethical concerns, the review proposes a more inclusive Ethics Guideline for AIED.
evidence: Based on the blank between existing ethical frameworks and ethic concerns from user's perspectives, the research proposes more inclusive and thoughtfully Ethics Guideline for AIED.

unit: The study recommends that multiple stakeholders adopt guidelines for AI in education that address user-centered concerns.
evidence: The study also provides actionable recommendations for multiple stakeholders, emphasizing the need for guidelines that address user-centered concerns.

unit: Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) is defined as the harnessing of AI to provide personalized and automated feedback in educational contexts.
evidence: The utilization of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED), defined as the harnessing of AI to provide personalized and automated feedback in educational contexts [5,6], is reshaping the educational domain [7-9].

unit: AIED covers diverse services including automatic essay scoring, learning analytics, intelligent tutoring systems, smart assistive technology, natural language processing, and autonomous pedagogical agents.
evidence: This transformation includes diverse educational services such as automatic essay scoring, learning analytics, intelligent tutoring systems, smart assistive tech, natural language processing, and autonomous pedagogical agents [7].

unit: AI ethics emphasizes human-centric values such as fairness, accountability, transparency, ethics, and safety, and concerns both public entities and private enterprises.
evidence: AI ethics emphasizes humancentric values such as fairness, accountability, transparency, ethics, and safety [12,13] and concerns both public entities and private enterprises [14].

unit: Participation in the global AI ethics debate is unequal: developing regions like Africa, South and Central America, and Central Asia are underrepresented while wealthier countries have disproportionate influence, raising concerns about neglect of local knowledge, cultural pluralism and global fairness.
evidence: Developing regions such as Africa, South and Central America, and Central Asia are underrepresented, while more economically developed countries have a disproportionate influence in shaping this debate. This imbalance reveals a power disparity in international discourse and raises concerns about the neglect of local knowledge, cultural pluralism, and the imperatives of global fairness [14], which creates substantial barriers to realizing the human-centric values that ethical AIED seeks to uphold for users.

unit: Extensive data collection and analysis in AI-based education raises serious human rights, ethical and legal questions, especially around personal data and learner autonomy.
evidence: Embracing AI in education involves extensive data collection and analysis across various educational landscapes, bringing about serious human rights, ethical, and legal questions, and escalating concerns, particularly around personal data and learner autonomy [7].

unit: Despite rapid AIED expansion, the field still lacks robust ethical guidelines for designing, developing and implementing reliable and accountable AI in education, and ethics literature in the AIED community has been scarce since Aiken and Epstein's early guidelines.
evidence: However, even with the accelerated expansion of AIED, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, the field still lacks robust ethical guidelines for crafting, developing, and implementing reliable and accountable AI within education [7,8].

unit: Existing frameworks and guidelines from international or national institutions are mostly generic across disciplines or overlook critical AIED ethical issues, so they may be insufficient for education at all levels and no consistent, comprehensive ethical approach exists.
evidence: While various frameworks, guidelines, and principles have been proposed by international or national institutions (see Table 1), most of these provide a relatively generic framework across disciplines and settings or fail to consider certain critical ethical issues about AIED. As such, they might not be appropriate, specific, and sufficient for education at all levels. There remains an absence of a consistent and comprehensive ethical approach to using AI in education.

unit: The release of ChatGPT at the end of 2022 triggered an AI revolution across society, particularly in higher education, while COVID-19 pushed institutions online and intensified debate about leveraging AI for remote and virtual learning.
evidence: However, it wasn't until the end of 2022, with the release of ChatGPT and its remarkable capabilities and accessibility, that an AI revolution truly seemed to sweep across every facet of society, particularly within the realm of higher education [4].

unit: Most existing international and national AI ethics frameworks are generic across disciplines and settings or ignore critical ethical issues specific to AI in education (AIED), so they may not be appropriate, specific, or sufficient for education at all levels.
evidence: While various frameworks, guidelines, and principles have been proposed by international or national institutions (see Table 1), most of these provide a relatively generic framework across disciplines and settings or fail to consider certain critical ethical issues about AIED. As such, they might not be appropriate, specific, and sufficient for education at all levels.

unit: There is currently no consistent and comprehensive ethical approach to using AI in education.
evidence: There remains an absence of a consistent and comprehensive ethical approach to using AI in education.

unit: Many educational technology companies and institutions have not prioritized AIED ethics, partly because stakeholders have limited awareness of AI's risks in education and because standard ethical guidelines are new to policymakers.
evidence: Moreover, the ethical considerations of AIED have not been a priority for many educational technology companies and institutions. One contributing factor is the limited awareness among relevant stakeholders about the potential risks of AI in the educational context [16].

unit: Users are increasingly concerned about the lack of transparency and oversight in AIED, making it essential and urgent to approach AI ethics in education from the user's perspective.
evidence: Coupled with the fact that establishing standard ethical guidelines for AIED is still relatively new for policymakers [41], concerns are growing among users about the lack of transparency and oversight. In this environment, understanding and approaching AI ethics in education from the user's perspective becomes both essential and urgent.

unit: Although AIED has been studied for over 30 years and has grown rapidly in the last decade, discourse on its ethics from the users' perspective has lagged behind.
evidence: Overall, while AIED has been an area of academic research for over 30 years [42,43], experiencing significant growth in the last decade [44], the discourse on its ethics especially from the perspective of users hasn't kept pace.

unit: Existing systematic reviews of AIED ethics cover many stakeholders and rely on meta-analyses or thematic analysis of principles, but they frequently lack a focused exploration of the users' perspective.
evidence: Emerging systematic literature reviews on AIED ethics concern a broad range of stakeholders, including users, policymakers, and developers, primarily focusing on ethical issues through meta-analyses [45] or exploring principles and their implications through thematic analysis [20]. However, they frequently lack a more focused exploration of the users' perspective.

unit: User-centered ethical guidelines for AIED can raise users' awareness of ethics, address their concerns, push ed-tech companies and institutions to attend to ethics, inform policymaking, and uphold human-centric values and sustainable growth of AIED.
evidence: aiming to devise more inclusive and thoughtfully constructed ethical guidelines for AIED from the perspective of users, which can help raise awareness of ethics in AIED among users, address their concerns, encourage greater attention to ethics from ed-tech companies and educational institutions, and inform better policymaking.

unit: Certain AI applications in education can create new ethical and legal challenges, including liability, biased decision-making, equity, reliability, academic honesty and plagiarism, privacy, transparency, algorithmic and content bias, and reduced human interaction.
evidence: While the integration of AI in education offers clear advantages, such as enhanced student engagement, collaboration, and greater accessibility, like all revolutionary technologies, certain AI applications can generate new ethical and legal challenges, especially around liability and potential biases in decision-making, raising concerns regarding ethics and equity, reliability, academic honesty and plagiarism, information privacy, transparency, algorithmic and content bias, and the possible reduction of human interaction [50, 51], which poses great threat to human-centric values associated with different stakeholders including developers and users at all levels and presents significant challenges to future development of AI in education.

unit: AIED ethics must address not only the data collection and computational ethics common to AI in general, but also the ethics of education, the needs of teachers and students, and ethical safeguards for AI-enhanced pedagogical activities, which makes the users' perspective important.
evidence: It is affirmed that, in addition to the ethical concerns related to the vast amounts of data collected and the computational approaches used, as with AI in general, AIED ethics must also address the ethics of education, the needs of teachers and students, and the ethical safeguards for AIED-enhanced pedagogical activities [21]. This highlights the importance of considering ethical AIED from the users' perspective.

unit: The COVID-19 pandemic pushed education online and made institutions rely heavily on ed-tech, which, with large data flows and corporate investment, accelerated demand for AI-driven remote learning solutions and is likely to sustain growth in AI-powered ed-tech.
evidence: The global outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic drastically shifted education towards online platforms, forcing institutions to rely heavily on ed-tech products to manage content, facilitate operations, and maintain communication with students. This influx of data, coupled with significant corporate investment, transformed the pandemic into a lucrative opportunity for educational technology, further accelerating the demand for AI-driven solutions that support remote learning.

unit: Existing AI ethics frameworks from international and national bodies are often too broad across disciplines or overlook ethical issues specific to AIED, so a consistent and comprehensive ethical approach for AI in education is still lacking.
evidence: Overall, although numerous frameworks, guidelines, and principles have been proposed by international and national institutions (see Table 1), many of these are either too broad across disciplines and settings or overlook key ethical issues specific to AIED. Consequently, they may not be fully suitable, specific, or adequate for education at all levels. A consistent and comprehensive ethical approach to the use of AI in education is still lacking.

unit: The development of general guidelines for AIED platforms remains in its infancy for many stakeholders in education, even though many international organizations and national institutions craft AI ethics models.
evidence: Table 1 illustrates that while numerous international organizations and technologically advanced national institutions are dedicated to crafting AI ethics models [58], the development of general guidelines for AIED platforms remains in its infancy for many stakeholders within the educational realm [41].

unit: UNESCO affirmed that AI development should be people-centered and that AI in education must be designed ethically, without discrimination, ensuring equity, transparency, and auditability, particularly in data collection, use and dissemination.
evidence: Nevertheless, it is noteworthy that UNESCO [34] pinpointed six challenges in achieving sustainable development of AIED [20], recommended actions to address the opportunities and challenges in education presented by AI, and affirmed AI development should be centered on people and AI in education must be designed ethically, without discrimination, ensuring equity, transparency, and auditability particularly in data collection, use and dissemination.

unit: The European Parliament emphasized that many users of AI in education are children and young people, a vulnerable group requiring special care and protection.
evidence: The European Parliament [40] also emphasized that many users of AI in education are children and young people, a vulnerable group that requires special care and protection.

unit: Many users of AI in education are children and young people, a vulnerable group that requires special care and protection, which makes addressing ethical challenges from the users' perspective necessary.
evidence: The European Parliament [40] also emphasized that many users of AI in education are children and young people, a vulnerable group that requires special care and protection. This underscores the necessity and importance of addressing these challenges from the users' perspective.

unit: Because most AIED platforms are run by private companies and standard AIED guidelines are still new for many policymakers, users are increasingly concerned about a lack of transparency and oversight.
evidence: Given that most AI in Education (AIED) platforms and tools are currently operated by private companies [63], and that the development of standard AIED guidelines is still a relatively new endeavor for many policymakers [41], users have growing concerns about the lack of transparency and oversight.

unit: Understanding AI ethics from the user's perspective can inform better policy decisions and address user concerns, contributing to the sustainable development of AIED.
evidence: Such an understanding can not only inform better policy decisions but also address user concerns, thus contributing to the sustainable development of AIED.

unit: Educators' willingness to integrate AI depends not only on the technology's accessibility and effectiveness but also on their readiness to accept its role in education.
evidence: The willingness of educators to integrate AI into their practices hinges not just on the technology's accessibility and effectiveness, but also on their readiness to accept its role in the educational landscape [8].

unit: Addressing ethical considerations enhances user confidence, and since trust is pivotal to technology adoption, this raises users' readiness to adopt AI-driven educational tools.
evidence: Trust plays a pivotal role in technology adoption [64], and by addressing ethical considerations, we can enhance user confidence and subsequently their readiness to adopt AI-driven tools in education [65].

unit: Earlier reviews of AI ethics, such as those on general principles, radiology and healthcare, gave limited attention to educational contexts.
evidence: Regarding emerging reviews on AI ethics, Jobin et al. [14] conducted a scoping review to examine global consensus and implementation of general ethical AI principles and guidelines. Yang et al. [66] focused specifically on radiology, while Mollmann et al. [67] conducted a systematic literature review centered on healthcare. However, all of these reviews gave limited attention to educational contexts.

unit: Ethics discourse in AIED remains underdeveloped, with consistent and comprehensive guidelines lacking and insufficient attention paid to users' perspectives.
evidence: A review of the existing literature reveals that the discourse on ethics in AIED remains underdeveloped, with consistent and comprehensive guidelines still lacking and insufficient attention given to users' perspectives.

unit: The Tripartite model for systematic literature reviews has three core elements: Descriptive (an overview of the literature), Synthesis (grouping research by common themes, linkages and underlying principles), and Critique (deep analysis to corroborate, refute, or introduce fresh perspectives).
evidence: The Tripartite model is structured around three core elements: Descriptive, which offers an overview of the literature; Synthesis, where research is grouped logically based on common themes, linkages, and underlying principles; and Critique, which involves a deep analysis of the literature to corroborate, refute, or introduce fresh perspectives.

unit: Ethical issues surrounding AI are no longer confined to science fiction; they are real issues affecting the education sector, where AI is actively deployed.
evidence: Ethical deliberations surrounding AI are no longer confined to the realm of science fiction; they are tangible issues influencing the educational sector where AI is actively deployed.

unit: Stakeholders in education such as teachers, students, researchers, libraries, and administrators are still in the early stages of understanding the ethical ramifications of AI, and are exploring how ethical frameworks can foster educational advancement.
evidence: Stakeholders such as teachers, students, researchers, libraries, and administrators are still in the early stages of grasping the ethical ramifications associated with AI. Moreover, they are exploring how these frameworks can be harnessed to foster advancements in education.

unit: Examining existing research on ethical frameworks from the viewpoint of AIED users can offer actionable strategies for optimal integration of AI in educational settings.
evidence: As such, examining the present research on ethical frameworks from the viewpoint of AIED users can offer actionable strategies for optimal AI integration in educational settings.

unit: The systematic review on AI ethics from users' perspective in education included articles that gave detailed descriptions and evaluations of AI ethics, or ethical applications of AI, from the user perspective in educational contexts.
evidence: Articles were selected if they provided detailed descriptions and evaluations of AI ethics, or ethical applications of AI, from the perspective of users in the educational context.

unit: The review excluded articles that mainly addressed ethics AI developers should follow, ethical strategies of large organizations or governments, purely theoretical frameworks, or theoretical curriculum design discussions.
evidence: Articles that primarily discussed ethics that AI development should adhere to, ethical strategies of large organizations or national governments, purely theoretical framework discussions, or theoretical discussions related to curriculum design, were excluded.

unit: The review synthesized users' ethical concerns about AI in education using content analysis and thematic analysis, and used critical analysis to assess the quality and relevance of outcomes in constructing an Ethics Guideline for AIED.
evidence: Qualitative methods were employed to analyze data. Descriptive statistics were analyzed to summarize key information of the reviewed literature, while content analysis [80] and thematic analysis [81] was utilized to synthesize existing frameworks, categorizing and comparing ethic concerns from users' perspectives, and critical analysis helped thoroughly assess the quality, validity, and relevance of the outcomes and then construct Ethics Guideline for AIED.

unit: The largest share of reviewed articles on AI ethics in education from the user perspective (35.29%) appeared in 2022, which may reflect the rapid advancement of AIED and growing reliance on AI in education, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: Most of the articles discussing ethics in AIED from the user perspective emerged in 2022, constituting over a third (35.29 %) of the total publications. This uptick may be attributed to the swift advancement of AIED and the escalating reliance on AI in education, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic [82].

unit: In the reviewed literature on user perspectives of AI ethics in education, more than half of articles (52.94%) focused on students' viewpoints, and about 17.65% included both students' and teachers' perspectives.
evidence: More than half (52.94 %) of these articles were centered on students' viewpoints, while approximately 17.65 % incorporated both students' and teachers' perspectives.

unit: Roughly half (52.94%) of the reviewed articles targeted higher education, while 23.53% addressed high school or middle school populations.
evidence: In terms of educational levels, roughly half of the articles (52.94 %) were aimed at higher education, while 23.53 % catered to the high school or middle school demographic.

unit: Most reviewed studies on user perspectives of AI ethics in education used qualitative methods (58.82%) such as interviews and case studies, while 29.41% used mainly questionnaire-based quantitative methods; only 17.65% had samples above 300.
evidence: Methodologically, a significant 58.82 % of the studies employed qualitative techniques-utilizing interviews, meetings, case studies, open-ended surveys, or observations-while 29.41 % used quantitative methods, primarily questionnaire surveys. However, only 17.65 % of these studies had sample sizes exceeding 300, just meeting the minimum threshold for enhanced generalizability [83].

unit: Only 23.53% of the reviewed articles used recognized international or national institutional ethical frameworks, whereas 11.76% relied on other researchers' theories and 35.29% created their own theoretical constructs.
evidence: Regarding theoretical underpinnings, 23.53 % of the articles turned to recognized international organizational and national institutional ethical frameworks. In contrast, some studies ventured without any predefined framework: 11.76 % relied on theories proposed by other researchers, and 35.29 % created their theoretical constructs.

unit: The "Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI" emerged as an early foundational ethical principle set for AI in education and was frequently cited in studies on accessibility, bias, and ethics of chatbots and educational intelligent agents.
evidence: Among the referenced frameworks, "Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI" emerged as an early foundational ethical principle for AIED. This guideline was frequently cited in articles that examined accessibility, biases, and ethics of chatbots and educational intelligent agents.

unit: The fifth provision of the Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI, together with WCAG 2.1, was used to address accessibility concerns in chatbots, conversational agents, and virtual assistants.
evidence: Specifically, the fifth provision of these ethics guidelines, in tandem with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1, was utilized to address accessibility concerns in chatbots, conversational agents, and virtual assistants [84].

unit: Researchers in the AIED community have observed a lack of cohesive frameworks for ethical concerns, and the 'strawman' draft framework for the ethics of AIED was created in response to this gap.
evidence: Several prominent researchers in the AIED community have observed a lack of cohesive frameworks to address ethical concerns in the field. Responding to this gap, a robust framework called the 'strawman' draft framework for the ethics of AIED was created [18].

unit: The extended UTAUT2 chatbot adoption model added four constructs, two of which concern chatbot ethics (perceived trust and ethics), to explain students' inclination to adopt chatbots.
evidence: Furthermore, an adoption model for chatbots termed the extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) Model, was introduced by incorporating four new constructs. Notably, two of these constructs focused on chatbot ethics, namely perceived trust and ethics. This model was employed to discern the factors influencing students' inclination to adopt chatbot technology.

unit: Although the extended UTAUT2 is not strictly an ethical framework, its expansion with ethics-related constructs shows the growing significance of AI ethics in future models.
evidence: Even though it wasn't strictly an ethical framework, the model's expansion underscores the growing significance of AI ethics in upcoming models [64].

unit: A model based on UNESCO's 2020 principles integrates deontological and utilitarian ethical frameworks to guide agent actions through ethical standards and to navigate ethical dilemmas in educational AI.
evidence: This model, which integrates both deontological and utilitarian ethical frameworks, aims to direct agent actions via ethical standards and to navigate ethical quandaries [85].

unit: Ethical issues in AI in education (AIED) from the perspective of users such as teachers, students, administrators, libraries and parents have been neglected in research, and where ethics is mentioned it is often covered only in a few sentences in the findings.
evidence: While concerns of ethics was mentioned in some studies, it was interesting that it was not covered in detail and often reported in the limited sentences in the findings.

unit: Students' ethical concerns about AI include perceived risks, AI-human relationships (supplanting humans, authorship, credit and copyright), trust in information quality and misinformation, unclear responsibility for AI decisions, dehumanization, explainability, transparency and fairness, data privacy and misuse, dataset bias, undefined regulation, plagiarism, and conflating AI with automation.
evidence: From the students' perspective, their concerns mainly include: 1) AI's perceived risks(81); 2) the relationsship between AI and humans, such as AI eventually supplanting humans and the potential adverse effects on an individual's social life, as well as safeguarding proper credit in collaboration with AI, grappling with matters of authorship, and broaching the boundaries of creative work copyrights (81, 77, 85); 3) trust in AI-derived quality of information and the potential for misinformation; 4) stakeholder responsibility and the absence of clarity on responsibility for AI-driven decisions (81, 86); 5) concerns of dehumanization and AI being devoid of emotions or causing physical harm (81, 86); 6) concerns of explainability, transparency, and fairness, such as seeking clarity of transparency in the data underpinning AI software and ensuring fairness (82, 87, 77); 7) concerns about maintaining data privacy and the potential misuse of data (83, 86, 87); 8) inherent biases in data sets toward women, visible minorities, individuals with disabilities, and indigenous populations (77, 86); 9) an undefined regulatory framework governing AI (87); 10) navigating issues of plagiarism and assessing the integrity of student writings (77); and 11) conflating AI with automation (86).

unit: Teachers share six ethical concerns about AI with students: transparency and fairness in decision-making, the AI-human relationship (including reduced teacher involvement, authorship and copyright), privacy risks, transparency in data underpinning AI, dataset bias, and plagiarism and writing integrity.
evidence: From the teachers' perspective, six concerns overlap with those mentioned by students: 1) transparency and fairness in AI decisionmaking processes(66,77), and 2) the relationship between AI and humans, with a potential scenario of increased AI presence and reduced teacher involvement(66), as well as safeguarding proper credit in collaboration with AI, grappling with matters of authorship, and broaching the boundaries of creative work copyrights(77); 3) potential privacy risks to both educators and learners due to data usage(66,77); 4) transparency and fairness in the data underpinning AI software(77); 5) inherent biases in data sets(77); and 6) issues of plagiarism and writing integrity(77).

unit: Teachers have six concerns distinct from students: loss of autonomy and control to AI, discrepancies between AI and teacher assessments, AI developers' lack of educational experience, AI's inability to grasp social, emotional and motivational factors, the perceived superiority of teachers' expertise and instinct over computer logic, and AI's ignorance of a student's external history.
evidence: At the same time, teachers also consider six concerns different from students' concerns. They are the shift of autonomy and control from teachers to AI, discrepancies between AI evaluations and teacher assessments, the dearth of educational experience among AI developers, the AI algorithms' inability to grasp social, emotional, and motivational facets, the perceived supremacy of teachers' real-world expertise and instinct over a computer's logic, and the AI systems' ignorance of a student's external history(66).

unit: Librarians' ethical concerns about AI largely align with students' and include data bias and filter bubbles, transparency of collection decisions, privacy, data quality and security of usage data, replacement of services by automation, and who drives information; the one concern not shared is the influence and methodology of data collection and its use for AI.
evidence: From the librarians' perspective, their concerns are consistent with those raised by students, include existing discussions about data bias and 'filter bubbles'; transparency issues concerning collection decisions; concerns about privacy, data quality, and security regarding usage data; the potential replacement of current services with automation; and deliberations over whether libraries or other entities would drive information(80). Only one has not been mentioned, that is, the influence and methodology associated with data collection and its utilization for AI(80).

unit: Studies of user perspectives on AI ethics in education mainly examine students' concerns, treating students as primary stakeholders because they are vulnerable to AI-driven educational interventions and directly exposed to the ethical challenges.
evidence: These studies explore students' perceptions, awareness, and the ethical implications of AIED, underscoring the significance of students as primary stakeholders. This emphasis is crucial given their vulnerability to AI-driven educational interventions and their direct exposure to the associated ethical challenges [13,64,84,85,96,97,98,99,100].

unit: Previous AIED-focused reviews address ethical issues for a broad range of stakeholders (policymakers, developers and users) but lack a focused exploration of the users' perspective, a gap this review fills.
evidence: While previous reviews that focus specifically on AIED tend to address ethical issues for a broad range of stakeholders, including policymakers, developers and users [20,68], they often lack a focused exploration of the users' perspective.

unit: Many other reviews on AIED development touch on ethical concerns but do not deeply investigate the essential elements of ethical AI, its implications and implementation, nor synthesize existing AIED frameworks and guidelines in terms of convergence, divergence, accomplishments and shortages.
evidence: Moreover, although many other reviews on AIED development touch on key ethical concerns regarding AI's role in education [70-75,101], they generally fail to provide an in-depth investigation of the essential elements that constitute ethical AI, its implication and the implementation for its realization, and fall short of offering a synthesized analysis of the existing frameworks and guidelines for AIED, particularly regarding their convergence, divergence, accomplishments and shortages.

unit: The review develops an Ethics Guideline for AIED from users' perspectives, for students, teachers/academics/researchers/experts and librarians, building on the Holmes et al. 'strawman' framework and adding the overlooked ethics of learning analytics and of algorithms.
evidence: This systematic review develops an Ethics Guideline for AIED from users' perspectives, aimed at guiding a wide array of users in AIED-including students, teachers/academics/researchers/experts, and librarians-in the ethical and reliable development and implementation of AIED systems; addressing overlooked ethical facets(the ethics of learning analytics and the ethics of Algorithm in AIED), based on the "strawman" draft framework presented by Holmes et al. [18].

unit: Unlike earlier global-consensus principles aimed at companies, research institutions and public-sector organizations, the new guideline is tailored to the needs and concerns of AIED users.
evidence: Unlike previous principles that sought to establish a global consensus on ethical AIED, who explored global agreement and the implementation of general principles, they primarily catered to a wide range of stakeholders, including private companies, research institutions, and public sector organizations [14], this guideline tailored to the unique needs and concerns of AIED users.

unit: Existing AIED ethical frameworks, principles and standards center on general data ethics in AI, i.e. where data ethics intersects with computational methods in education.
evidence: It is obvious that the ethical components of the eight pre-existing ethical frameworks, principles, and standards tailored for AIED have been centered around data ethics, computational methods, and education, specifically at the juncture where data ethics intersects with computational methods.

unit: Many contemporary AIED ethical frameworks fail to address the ethics of learning analytics, even though it is a heavily researched area.
evidence: However, the ethical facets of learning analytics, a subject of significant research [90], often go unaddressed in many contemporary AIED ethical frameworks.

unit: User-raised ethical concerns missing from established AIED frameworks include mutual respect between AI and humans, the rights and emotions of AI/robots, and reconciling differences between AI's diagnosis and a teacher's perspective.
evidence: Some of these concerns include the mutual respect between AI and humans [92], gearing AI to comprehend education better [1], acknowledging the rights and emotions of AI/robots [93], and reconciling differences between AI's diagnosis and a teacher's perspective.

unit: Users also raised concerns that AI developers may lack educational experience, that algorithms cannot grasp social, emotional and motivational factors, that teachers' real-world intuition is superior to AI, and that algorithms may be unaware of a student's history outside the system.
evidence: Other issues touched on the potential deficiencies of AI developers in the educational experience, AI algorithms' inability to grasp social, emotional, and motivational factors, and the perceived superiority of a teacher's real-world experience and intuition over AI. There's also the challenge that AI algorithms may be unaware of a student's history outside the system [65].

unit: Authorship, copyright for creative works, and diverse perceptions of AI's constraints on human understanding are user-raised ethical challenges not adequately covered by existing AIED frameworks.
evidence: Moreover, challenges like diverse perceptions of AI's constraints on human understanding, matters of authorship, and copyright parameters for creative works also emerge [87].

unit: The ethical issues overlooked in existing AIED frameworks fall into two categories: the ethics of learning analytics (data ethics meets education) and the ethics of algorithms in AIED (computational methods meet education).
evidence: These overlooked ethical facets fall primarily into two categories (the ethics of learning analytics and the ethics of Algorithm in AIED). The first pertains to the intersection of data ethics and education, which can be termed the ethics of learning analytics, as highlighted by Ref. [94], Drachsler and Greller [95], and Ferguson et al. unit: Discrepancies exist between prevailing AIED ethical frameworks and the actual ethical challenges users face, so the authors built on Holmes et al.'s framework to construct an Ethics Guideline for AIED from users' perspectives.
evidence: From the detailed analysis above, it becomes evident that there are discrepancies between prevailing ethical frameworks and the actual ethical challenges faced in AIED from users' perspectives.
