section_path: Chapter 1 Responsible AI and AI Governance

unit: The four SAFE-HAI statistical trustworthiness measures are all based on an extension of the Lorenz curve, which was introduced by Max Lorenz in 1905 to assess economic inequality and was summarized by Corrado Gini as the Gini index.
evidence: From a methodological viewpoint, the statistical metrics that are proposed in the SAFE-HAI framework consist of a set of four integrated statistical measures of trustworthiness, all based on the extension of the Lorenz curve. 15
section_path: Chapter 1 Responsible AI and AI Governance

unit: The Lorenz curve can measure the contribution of each training data point or explanatory variable to an ML model's output, and thereby inequalities in dimensions such as security, fairness, or accuracy (distance from ground truth).
evidence: The Lorenz curve is an appropriate tool to measure the contribution of each individual data point in the training data to the output of an ML model, in order to assess the inequalities of single data points or groups of points, and to measure the distance of the output from the ground truth.
section_path: Chapter 1 Responsible AI and AI Governance

unit: A particular Lorenz curve or Gini index value for AI output is not inherently good or bad; it must be compared with benchmarks or thresholds set by regulators, policy makers, developers, or calculated statistically.
evidence: As for income and wealth, a specific Lorenz curve and Gini index value does not necessarily imply a positive or a negative statement on the AI output. This is dependent on the comparison between the obtained values and some reference benchmarks and threshold which can be set by regulators and policy makers or by AI developers themselves, or calculated statistically.
section_path: Chapter 1 Responsible AI and AI Governance

unit: In the SAFE-HAI framework, accuracy is measured by comparing the Lorenz curve of the true response with a curve built from the ranks of the model's predictions, yielding the Rank Graduation Accuracy (RGA) measure.
evidence: Accuracy will be measured by comparing the Lorenz curve of the true response with a similar curve obtained using the ranks of the predictions provided by the model, leading to the Rank Graduation Accuracy (RGA) measure.
section_path: Chapter 1 Responsible AI and AI Governance

unit: In SAFE-HAI, security is measured by comparing the Lorenz curve of the predictions with one built from the ranks of predictions obtained on perturbed data, yielding the Rank Graduation Robustness (RGR) measure.
evidence: Security will be measured by comparing the Lorenz curve of the predictions with a similar curve obtained using the ranks of the predictions obtained with the perturbed data, leading to the Rank Graduation Robustness (RGR) measure.
section_path: Chapter 1 Responsible AI and AI Governance

unit: In SAFE-HAI, the explainability of an input variable is measured by comparing the Lorenz curve of the predictions with one obtained using all input variables except the one examined, yielding the Rank Graduation Explainability (RGE) measure.
evidence: Explainability of an input variable will be measured by comparing the Lorenz curve of the predictions with a similar curve obtained using all input variables except the one under examination, leading to the Rank Graduation Explainability (RGE) measure.
section_path: Chapter 1 Responsible AI and AI Governance

unit: In SAFE-HAI, fairness of a protected variable is measured like explainability, by comparing Lorenz curves of predictions for each population group in the protected variable, yielding the Rank Graduation Fairness (RGF) measure.
evidence: Fairness of a (protected) input variable will be measured in a similar way as explainability, by comparing the Lorenz curve of the predictions for each population group contained in the protected variable, leading to a Rank Graduation Fairness (RGF) measure.
section_path: Chapter 1 Responsible AI and AI Governance

unit: In SAFE-HAI, privacy is measured by how the Lorenz curve of predictions changes when one or more records are forgotten, yielding the Rank Graduation Privacy (RGP) measure.
evidence: Privacy will measure how the Lorenz curve of the predictions varies when it "forgets" (eliminates) one or more records, leading to a Rank Graduation Privacy (RGP) measure.
section_path: Chapter 1 Responsible AI and AI Governance

unit: In SAFE-HAI, environmental sustainability is measured through the explainability of specific environmental, social and governance factors (RGS), and human-in-the-loop is measured by the impact of human interventions on AI output (RGH).
evidence: Environmental sustainability will measure the explainability of specific environmental (but also social and governance) factors, leading to a Rank Graduation Sustainability (RGS) measure.
section_path: Chapter 1 Responsible AI and AI Governance

unit: The authors argue that applying the Lorenz curve methodology to AI output yields SAFE-HAI metrics that fit the requirements of recommendations and regulations such as the US AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act, and can also derive further compliance metrics for qualitative aspects like privacy, sustainability and HITL impact.
evidence: The Lorenz curve methodology can also be employed to derive further compliance metrics and evaluate the qualitative aspects of the AI output, such as privacy preservation, environmental sustainability, and the impact of HITL.
section_path: Chapter 1 Responsible AI and AI Governance

unit: Extending the Lorenz curve to AI output provides a user-friendly tool for assessing AI systems across dimensions in an agnostic and transparent way.
evidence: In summary, the extension of the Lorenz curve to the AI output can provide a user-friendly tool designed to assess AI systems across different dimensions in an agnostic and transparent way.
section_path: Chapter 1 Responsible AI and AI Governance

unit: Accuracy is a key metric and principle in AI development, in which a model's performance is tested and measured before its release.
evidence: Accuracy is a key metric and principle in AI development, in which the performance of a model is tested and measured before its release.

unit: Accuracy is a key part of the SAFE-HAI framework and a crucial Responsible AI principle, and the SAFE-HAI framework is critical to building AI algorithms that adhere to new AI policies.
evidence: We also introduced the SAFE-HAI framework which is critical to achieving responsibly built AI algorithms that adheres to the newly introduced AI policies. In this chapter, we'll review "accuracy," a key part of the SAFE-HAI framework and a crucial Responsible AI principle.

unit: Incorrect or inaccurate outputs from AI applications, including LLMs and generative AI, are typically observed even though the models have undergone several performance tests.
evidence: In most cases, when incorrect and inaccurate outputs of an AI application have been observed, including those from large language models (LLMs) and generative AI, the performance of these models/applications would have undergone several performance tests.

unit: It is always recommended to measure the accuracy of any AI model or application, using accuracy metrics and measurements as part of development, to ensure its outputs are fair and accurate.
evidence: Running performance tests through accuracy metrics and measurements is part of AI development. It's always recommended to measure the accuracy of any given AI model/application to ensure the outputs are fair and accurate.

unit: The EU AI Act requires all high-risk AI systems to have an appropriate level of accuracy in their design and development, with consistent performance throughout the model's life cycle.
evidence: The AIA's requirements for high-risk systems, described in Chapter 1, stipulate that all high-risk AI systems need to have an appropriate level of accuracy in their design and development, with a consistent performance throughout the model(s) life cycle.

unit: Under the EU AI Act, benchmarks and measurement methodologies must be developed to measure appropriate accuracy levels, and the accuracy levels and relevant metrics must be declared in the manual or instructions of use.
evidence: The development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies are required in order to measure the appropriate levels of accuracy. As part of the AIA, the levels of accuracy and relevant accuracy metrics need to be declared in the manual/ instructions of use.

unit: In the NIST risk management framework, accuracy is a trustworthy AI characteristic, requiring AI to be valid and reliable.
evidence: According to the NIST risk management framework, accuracy is one of the trustworthy AI characteristics that AI systems are required to have, where AI should be valid and reliable.

unit: NIST defines validation as confirmation, through objective evidence, that the requirements for a specific intended use or application have been fulfilled.
evidence: Validation here refers to the "confirmation, through the provision of objective evidence, that the requirements for a specific intended use or application have been fulfilled."

unit: A valid AI application must be accurate, while a reliable AI application must be robust.
evidence: A valid AI application must be accurate, whereas a reliable AI application must be robust.

unit: NIST recommends considering three questions when measuring ML model accuracy: how accuracy will be assessed, which benchmarks will be used, and how it will be communicated.
evidence: There are a few questions the NIST recommends to consider when measuring the accuracy of an ML model:

unit: Accuracy can be categorized as an organizational risk rather than a human risk, because it affects model performance and thus the organization that owns and builds the model before reaching the end user.
evidence: Breaking it down further, we can categorize accuracy as an organizational risk as opposed to a human risk, where it affects the performance of the model, subsequently affecting the organization that owns, builds, and develops the model before the end user.

unit: Simpler models such as regression models are typically less accurate than more complex models such as neural networks, and accuracy measurement must distinguish numerical from categorical responses and structured-data ML from unstructured-data LLMs.
evidence: Typically, simpler models (e.g., regression models) are less accurate than more complex models (e.g., neural network models). To measure accuracy, we should distinguish the case of numerical response variables (prediction problems) from that of categorical response variables (classification problems). We should also distinguish the case of machine learning models based on structured data from the case of large language models based on unstructured data.

unit: Two benchmark metrics measure the distance between predicted and true output: Rank Graduation Accuracy (RGA) for models on structured data, and the TrustGPT benchmark for large language models on unstructured data.
evidence: In this chapter, we'll describe two main benchmark metrics from a statistical point of view: the Rank Graduation Accuracy (RGA) metrics, 18, 19 which measures the "distance" between the predicted output and the true (or expected) output, for models based on structured data, and the TrustGPT benchmark, 20 which measures a similar distance, for large language models based on unstructured data.

unit: For numerical target variables, accuracy is measured by the distance between predictions and ground truth, most commonly via mean squared error (MSE), the arithmetic mean of squared differences between predicted and true values.
evidence: When the target response variable is numerical, accuracy measures rely on the distance between the predictions and the ground truth values; the most common are based on the mean squared error (MSE).

unit: The mean error can mislead because negative and positive errors offset each other, so squaring errors before averaging (MSE) is used instead.
evidence: The mean error can be, however, misleading, as negative errors may compensate for positive errors, and vice versa. For this reason, we calculate the mean of the squared errors, leading to the mean squared error which, in the example, turns out to be equal to about 54.90.

unit: RMSE, the square root of MSE, is customarily used because it returns the accuracy metric to the original scale of the values rather than squared units.
evidence: From an interpretational viewpoint, the mean squared error may not be appropriate, as it squares the original scale of the ROE. For this reason, it is customary to consider RMSE (root mean squared error), which is the square root of the mean square error, which brings back the accuracy metrics to the scale of the considered values (percentages in the example, rather than squared percentages).

unit: In the ROE prediction example, an RMSE of about 7.41 is very large relative to the mean actual ROE, indicating the model's output is not very accurate.
evidence: For the considered example, RMSE is equal to about 7.41 - a very large value compared to the mean of the actual ROE. This indicates that, for this simple example, the AI output is not very accurate.

unit: RMSE corresponds to the Euclidean distance between the vector of predicted values and the ground truth, i.e., the classic geometric distance.
evidence: From a more mathematical viewpoint, the RMSE corresponds to the Euclidean distance of the vector of predicted values from the ground truth. Euclidean distance refers to the classic standard geometric distance, such as the distance between two cities.

unit: The Choice of Plausible Alternatives (COPA) benchmark is a causal reasoning task in which the model must discern the cause or effect within a sentence.
evidence: Choice of Plausible Alternatives (COPA): A causal reasoning task where the model is tasked to discern the cause or effect within a sentence.

unit: The Winograd Schema Challenge (WSC) is a coreference resolution task where the system must pick the correct referent of a pronoun in a sentence from a list of noun phrases.
evidence: Winograd Schema Challenge (WSC): Consists of a coreference resolution task with examples that have a sentence with a pronoun and a list of noun phrases from the sentence. The system is tasked to select the correct referent of the pronoun from the provided multiple choices.

unit: Word-in-Context (WIC) is a binary classification task on sentence pairs in which the model decides whether a polysemous word is used with the same intent in both sentences.
evidence: Word-in-Context (WIC): A binary classification of sentence pairs, where the model's task is to determine whether a word is used with the same intent in both sentences, when given two text snippets and a polysemous word that appears in both sentences.

unit: Many benchmarks and research frameworks exist for evaluating LLMs, including HELM, LM Evaluation Harness, PromptBench, Chatbot Arena, SQuAD and IMDB.
evidence: There are so many other benchmarks and research frameworks available for LLMs, such as the HELM (Holistic Evaluation of Language Models) by Stanford University, LM Evaluation Harness by Eleuther AI, PromptBench by Microsoft, Chatbot Arena by LMSys.org, SQuAD for question-answering tasks, and IMDB for sentiment analysis.

unit: Practitioners should identify and run a couple of benchmarks suited to their use case and AI version to test model accuracy.
evidence: Depending on the use case and version of AI you're working with, it's important to identify and run a couple of benchmarks to test the accuracy of your model(s).

unit: Benchmarks are useful for checking compliance of AI applications but cannot simply be used in a risk management model; statistical metrics such as RGA are needed for that.
evidence: It is important to underline that, while very useful to check the compliance of AI applications, benchmarks cannot be simply used in a risk management model. To do so, statistical metrics such as RGA are necessary.

unit: Using one or more benchmarks to test compliance with the various Responsible AI principles is best practice and highly recommended.
evidence: However, ensuring the use of a benchmark or multiple benchmarks to test the compliance for various Responsible AI principles is best practice and highly recommended.

unit: When a large language model produces textual output, there is often no ground truth benchmark for accuracy, so accuracy metrics are more subjective and require more human intervention.
evidence: When the output is a textual response, as in large language models, we do not always have a ground truth as a benchmark against which to measure the accuracy of the output. In this case, accuracy metrics still exist, although they are more subjective and require a higher degree of human intervention.

unit: Huang et al. propose evaluating LLM output on three negative characteristics: toxicity, bias, and value alignment.
evidence: The authors propose to measure three negative characteristics for the output of large language models: their toxicity, their bias, and their value alignment.

unit: Toxicity of an LLM is the generation of rude, disrespectful, or unreasonable text, measured as the percentage of toxic outputs when the model is prompted to say something bad about a list of social norms.
evidence: Toxicity is defined as the generation of rude, disrespectful, or unreasonable text and is measured by calculating the percentage of toxic outputs among a given list of social norms which are prompted to the model, asking to say something bad about them.

unit: Bias in an LLM is measured as the difference in toxicity when the same questions are asked about different population groups; large variation in toxicity indicates bias.
evidence: Bias is the difference in toxicity when the same previous questions are asked to different population groups; a large variation in toxicity indicates bias.

unit: Value alignment is measured by asking the model to evaluate positive or negative descriptions of a social norm and calculating the percentage of discordant answers.
evidence: Finally, value alignment is measured by asking the model to evaluate a positive or negative description of a social norm and measuring the percentage of times in which the answer is discordant (i.e., negative when the description is positive and vice versa).

unit: The Mann-Whitney statistic is equivalent to the AUROC and more generally to the RGA metrics, so RGA can be used to measure AI model accuracy in all situations.
evidence: It's important to note the Mann-Whitney statistics is equivalent to the AUROC and, more generally, to the RGA metrics that we have proposed before. Thus, the proposed RGA statistics can be employed to measure the accuracy of AI models, in all situations.

unit: Hallucination is the generation of text that is incorrect or does not align with the given context; the Hallucination index evaluates it by computing mean AUROC across question-evidence-answer triples.
evidence: For example, it can be applied to the evaluation of "hallucination," that is, the generation of text that is incorrect, that is, does not align with the given context. A popular evaluation tool for this example is the Hallucination index, which calculates the mean AUROC in different triples of questions-evidence-answers.

unit: SuperGLUE was created as a harder successor to GLUE because LLMs surpassed non-expert human annotators on GLUE, leaving little room for further research.
evidence: SuperGLUE was introduced about a year after GLUE was launched in 2019 as the new introduction of large language models (LLMs) surpassed the level of non-expert human annotators, making the benchmark a bit redundant, with little room for further research.

unit: Communicating an ML model's performance and accuracy clearly, concisely and simply supports the Responsible AI principle of transparency and can raise the trust consumers and users place in the system.
evidence: This is important as it addresses "transparency" which is an important Responsible AI principle and could help improve the trust index of consumers and users.

unit: Poor accuracy in an ML model, such as one that identifies fraudulent claims, can lead to falsely accusing innocent people, which can cause reputational damage, lawsuits and regulatory fines.
evidence: The accuracy of your model could potentially make or break your business, for example, if you have an ML model that identifies fraudulent claims and the accuracy of your model is poor, it means that you could be falsely accusing innocent people of fraudulent claims. unit: To improve a poorly performing model, practitioners can increase the amount of training data, increase the number of variables to improve feature processing, and tune model parameters; more data raises cost unless synthetic data is used.
evidence: Increase the number of data in your training set. The more examples, the more accurate the model's performance will be. The only caveat to note is increased data equals increased cost, unless using synthetic data.

unit: A model underfits when it performs poorly on training data, and overfits when it performs well on training data but poorly on evaluation data, usually because it memorized the training data and cannot generalize to unseen examples.
evidence: Your model is "underfitting" when it performs poorly on the training data, and it's "overfitting" when on the flip side, it performs well on the training data, but poorly on the evaluation data. When this happens, it's usually due to memorization of the data it's been trained on, and the model is unable to generalize unseen examples.
section_path: How Will You Communicate This As Needed?

unit: Underfitting is addressed by increasing model flexibility and reducing regularization, while overfitting is addressed by reducing model flexibility (fewer feature combinations, smaller n-gram size) or increasing regularization.
evidence: Underfitting can be resolved by increasing the model flexibility and reduction of the amount of regularization used. Regularization refers to a set of techniques used to reduce model complexity and increase generalization which improves model accuracy. To solve overfitting, reduce the model flexibility through less feature combinations, n-grams size, or increase the amount of regularization used.
section_path: How Will You Communicate This As Needed?

unit: Feature processing is the selection, manipulation and transformation of raw data into features used in supervised learning.
evidence: Feature processing refers to the selection, manipulation, and transformation of raw data into features used in supervised learning.

unit: Robustness is the sturdiness of an ML model in withstanding uncertainties such as perturbations, adversarial conditions or cyber attacks, and in performing accurately across different contexts.
evidence: Robustness refers to the sturdiness of an ML model to withstand uncertainties (perturbations or adversarial conditions) such as cyber attacks, and the ability to perform accurately in different contexts.

unit: Building robust ML models is considered critical, not just advisable, because of ongoing systemic risks identified in AI systems, particularly generative AI.
evidence: Given the current concerns and unending systemic risks identified in AI systems, particularly generative AI, building robust ML models is not only advised but critical.

unit: Robustness is a fundamental principle of Responsible AI and of AI performance in general, and it is one of the principles in the SAFE-HAI framework.
evidence: Robustness is another fundamental and important principle of Responsible AI and AI performance in general.

unit: Under NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, an AI system must be trustworthy, and a key characteristic of trustworthiness is being valid and reliable.
evidence: According to NIST's RMF, an AI system has to be trustworthy. To achieve trustworthiness, one of the important characteristics is to have "valid and reliable" AI systems.

unit: Reliable AI systems are those that perform as intended without failure over a given period of time under specific conditions.
evidence: These are reliable systems that have the ability to perform as intended without potential failure over a given period of time, under specific conditions.

unit: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022 defines robustness, also called generalizability, as the ability of a system to maintain its level of performance under a variety of circumstances.
evidence: the ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022 defines robustness or generalizability as the "ability of a system to maintain its level of performance under a variety of circumstances."

unit: In NIST's risk management framework, robustness and accuracy are key characteristics an AI system needs to be considered trustworthy and reliable, and reliability means performing as required, without failure, for a given time interval under given conditions.
evidence: In NIST's risk management framework, robustness, along with accuracy, is a key characteristic an AI application/system should have to be considered trustworthy and, specifically, reliable. Reliability is defined as the "ability of an item to perform as required, without failure, for a given time interval, under given conditions."

unit: A valid AI application should be accurate, whereas a reliable AI application must be robust.
evidence: While a valid AI application should be accurate, a reliable AI application must be robust.

unit: Safety aims to avoid harms to the health of people, property, and the environment, while security aims to avoid unauthorized access to data, such as through adversarial attacks and data poisoning.
evidence: Safety aims to avoid harms that affect the health of people, property, and the environment. Security, on the other hand, aims to avoid unauthorized access of data such as adversarial attacks and data poisoning.

unit: Security is directly tied to robustness through its consequences for reliability, while safety is an indirect consequence of lack of robustness, which leads to unexpected harms to people and the environment.
evidence: Security is directly related to the notion of robustness and specifies its consequences in terms of reliability of an AI application, that is, the expectation that it works as expected, whereas safety can be seen as an indirect consequence of lack of robustness, which leads to unexpected harms on people and the environment.

unit: The EU AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to have an appropriate level of robustness and cybersecurity so they perform consistently throughout their life cycle.
evidence: The EU AI Act also refers to robustness and the requirement to ensure that high-risk AI systems have an appropriate level of robustness and cybersecurity in order to perform consistently throughout the life cycle of an AI system.

unit: Robustness is measured by how much a machine learning model's output varies under data perturbations, which may be intentional (cyber attacks) or unintentional (extreme rare events); a model is robust when this variation is limited.
evidence: The measurement of robustness draws on the variation of the output of a machine learning model caused by data perturbations, generated intentionally (as in cyber attacks) or unintentionally (as in extreme rare events). A model is robust when the variation of its output under a data perturbation is limited, and it's not robust otherwise.

unit: For classification problems, a classifier is robust if it correctly classifies a large proportion of cases under all possible variations of the input variables within a certain distance.
evidence: A more precise definition of robustness can be stated for classification problems: a classifier is robust if it correctly classifies a large proportion of cases, under all possible variations of the input variables (within a certain distance, see, e.g., Croce et al., 2023).

unit: Simpler models with fewer explanatory variables tend to be more robust than complex models with more features because they have fewer sources of anomalous variation; this reflects the bias-variance trade-off, where simple models have higher bias but lower variance.
evidence: Typically, simpler models with fewer explanatory variables are more robust than more complex models, with more feature variables, as the sources of anomalous variation are less in the former case. This aspect is also known as the bias-variance trade-off (see, e.g., Hastie et al., 2023), 27 where simple models have more bias than complex models, but lower variance.

unit: Robustness measurement has two related aspects: direct (ex post) measurement of output variability under data perturbations, and indirect (ex ante, by design) measurement via model comparison and regularization to select a model with an appropriate bias-variance trade-off.
evidence: In the measurement of robustness, we will thus consider two apparently distinct but related aspects: a direct measurement of robustness (ex post), in terms of output variability under data perturbations, and an indirect measurement of robustness (ex ante, by design), in terms of model comparison and regularization, which leads to the selection of a model with an appropriate bias-variance trade-off.

unit: The RGR metric (Giudici and Raffinetti) measures the distance between predicted output and predicted output under perturbations for structured-data models, while RobustBench (Croce et al.) measures a similar distance for large language models using unstructured data.
evidence: The development of this chapter is based on two main benchmark metrics: the RGR metrics, introduced by Giudici and Raffinetti (2024), 28 which measures the "distance" between the predicted output and the predicted output under perturbations, for models based on structured data, and the RobustBench metrics, developed by Croce et al. (2023), which measures a similar distance, for large language models based on unstructured data.

unit: For a continuous response, robustness can be assessed by resampling the train-test partition to get repeated predictions, then computing their mean, variance and percentiles; the variance shows how stable predictions are to changes in the underlying samples.
evidence: For a continuous response, we can resample the train-test partition and obtain repeated predictions, one for each sample. We can then calculate the mean of the predictions, as well as their variance, which measures how robust the predictions are by changing the underlying samples.

unit: A percentile of repeated predictions can serve as a decision threshold: if the 5th percentile of predictions is above zero, then at least 95% of predicted values are above zero, so the prediction is significantly higher than zero.
evidence: For example, if we repeat machine learning on different samples, to predict the value of a specific observation, the prediction will be significantly higher than zero if the 5th percentile is greater than zero, which means that at least 95% of the predicted values are above zero.

unit: For binary or ordinal responses, entropy or the Gini index can replace variance as measures of variability for categorical variables when assessing robustness.
evidence: For a binary or ordinal response, we can use the entropy or the Gini index, instead of the variance, which are both measures of variability for categorical variables.

unit: Explainability is a more recent Responsible AI principle than accuracy and robustness, and its importance has grown alongside the development of black-box learning models that can be very accurate but are very difficult or impossible to interpret.
evidence: While the principles of accuracy and robustness have been present for a relatively long time span, the notion of explainability is more recent. Its importance has grown in parallel with the development of "black-box" learning models that may be very accurate, although very difficult, or impossible, to interpret, especially in terms of their driving mechanisms.

unit: No precise mathematical definition of explainability exists because its interpretation is somewhat subjective, so the literature relies on regulatory definitions such as that of Bracke et al. (2019), which requires an explicit understanding of the factors that determine a given machine learning output.
evidence: While a precise mathematical definition of explainability is not available due to its somehow subjective interpretation, the extant literature relies on regulatory definitions, such as that reported in Bracke et al. (2019), 32 where explainability requires an explicit understanding of the factors which determine a given machine learning output.

unit: Under NIST's AI RMF, an AI system must be both explainable and interpretable: explainability refers to the mechanisms underlying AI systems, while interpretability refers to the meaning of AI output in the context of its designed purpose.
evidence: According to NIST's RMF, an AI system has to be explainable and interpretable. Explainable and interpretable artificial intelligence systems offer information that can help users understand the purposes and impact of AI systems, while interpretability refers to the meaning of AI output in the context of its designed purpose. Explainability refers to the mechanisms which underlay AI systems.

unit: The risk associated with explainability or interpretability stems from a lack of ability to make sense of an AI system's output.
evidence: The underlying assumption is that a risk of explainability or interpretability stems from a lack of ability to make sense of a system's output.

unit: AI systems must be explainable and interpretable in order to achieve trustworthiness.
evidence: To achieve trustworthiness, AI systems must be explainable and interpretable.

unit: The EU AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to be sufficiently transparent that deployers can interpret the system's output and use it appropriately, which ties its notion of transparency to explainability and interpretability.
evidence: The act states that "High risk AI systems should be designed and developed in a way to ensure their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret the system's output and use it appropriately." The notion of transparency adopted by the AI Act is clearly related to the notions of explainability and interpretability as previously defined.

unit: The EU AI Act's human oversight requirement also relates to explainability: AI systems must be designed so natural persons can effectively oversee them while in use.
evidence: Another reference of the AI Act to explainability can be found in the requirement of "human oversight." "AI systems must be designed and developed in such a way that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which the system is in use."

unit: Some machine learning models, such as linear and logistic regression, are explainable by design, while tree-based models like random forests and boosting are less explainable but offer a built-in feature importance plot that measures each variable's importance through the splits it generates.
evidence: Indeed, some machine learning models are explainable by design and don't need further refinements to be explainable. For example, linear and logistic regression have made recent advances thanks to feature selection optimization methods such as Lasso and Ridge. Other models such as tree models, random forests, bagging, and boosting models are much less explainable. However, these models have a built-in mechanism referred to as the feature importance plot that calculates the importance of each variable in terms of the splits (or average splits) it generates on the tree (or forest) model.

unit: Complex models such as neural networks and support vector machines are typically unexplainable, but this can be addressed with computational effort by permuting or reshuffling the values of an explanatory variable.
evidence: We also have more complex models such as neural networks and support vector machines that are typically unexplainable. This problem, however, can be solved with some computational efforts, by permuting and/or reshuffling the values of any given explanatory variable.

unit: Shapley values and their normalized variant, Shapley Lorenz values, are the most important model-agnostic post-processing measures for comparing the explainability of different machine learning models such as regressions, tree models, and neural networks.
evidence: Further research development has been motivated by the need to compare the explainability of different machine learning models, such as regressions, tree model, and neural networks, in terms of an independent model-agnostic measure run in a post-processing step. The most important of such measures are Shapley values (see, e.g., Shapley, 1953, 34 Lundberg, 2017 35 ) and their normalized variant, the Shapley Lorenz values (Giudici and Raffinetti, 2021 36 ).

unit: Shapley values originated in game theory to divide a game's value among participants and were extended to machine learning to equitably distribute a model's prediction among its regressors.
evidence: Shapley values were introduced in game theory with the aim of dividing the value of a game equally between the various participants. The goal was to extend the technique to machine learning models. In this context, Shapley values allow for the equitable distribution of a model's prediction among the regressors that constitute it.

unit: A Shapley value measures the added value of a variable to the prediction for each observation, and the global contribution of a variable is obtained by summing or averaging these values over all observations.
evidence:
In other words, Shapley value measures the added value of a variable, k, to the prediction of each observation.

Once Shapley values are calculated, the global contribution of each explanatory variable to the predictions is obtained by summing or averaging them over all observations.

unit: Shapley values help developers understand which explanatory variable drives a model's predictions.
evidence: Shapley values help developers understand the impact of the various explanatory variables in a model's output. In other words, they help you understand which explanatory variable drives the model's predictions.

unit: Lasso and Ridge regularization are applied during model building (ex ante) and mainly serve model selection, whereas Shapley values are applied after a model is selected (ex post) and serve model interpretation.
evidence: Unlike various regularization techniques, such as Lasso and Ridge, which are applied in model building (ex ante), Shapley values are applied once a model is selected (ex post). While Lasso and Ridge are mainly used for model selection, Shapley values are employed for model interpretation.

unit: If a smaller set of predictors explains enough of the response variability, choosing it makes the model more robust to input variations.
evidence: If a smaller set of predictors is sufficient, we can choose that, making the model more robust to input variations.

unit: Giudici and Raffinetti (2021) introduced Shapley Lorenz values, which replace the Shapley payoff with a payoff based on the difference between Gini coefficients (Lorenz Zonoids), normalized by definition.
evidence: To this aim, Giudici and Raffinetti (2021) introduced Shapley Lorenz values, which replace the payoff for Shapley values with a payoff based on the difference between Gini coefficients (Lorenz Zonoids), normalized by definition.

unit: Shapley values and Shapley Lorenz values are postprocessing techniques for judging whether a machine learning model is explainable and which variables mostly explain the variability of the predicted response.
evidence: Shapley values and Shapley Lorenz values are examples of postprocessing techniques that can be employed to understand whether a machine learning model is explainable and, if so, what are the variables that mostly explain the variability of the response to be predicted.

unit: Shapley-type postprocessing explainability measures can be computationally complex with many variables, because the number of possible variable combinations grows rapidly as variables increase.
evidence: While appealing, these measures, and similar post-processing techniques, may be computationally complex, especially when many variables are being considered. This is because the large number of possible combinations C becomes rapidly very large, as the number of variables increases.

unit: The chapter proposes the Rank Graduation Explainability measure (RGE), based on the Lorenz curve, to assess explainability and identify when an AI system is not explainable, similar to the accuracy and robustness metrics from earlier chapters.
evidence: To improve the assessment of explainability, in the next section we will propose a measure based on the Lorenz curve notion, similar to the accuracy and robustness metrics discussed in the previous chapters.

unit: The variable importance plot is one of the best-known methods for obtaining variable explanations for ensemble tree models such as random forest and gradient boosting.
evidence: Figure 4-2 exemplifies the application of one of the most known methods to obtain variable explanations for the family of ensemble tree models, which contains random forest and gradient boosting, for example, the variable importance plot described below.

unit: An AI application is deemed explainable if the complement to one of the sum of the RGE values is significantly higher than a subjectively determined bound.
evidence: An AI application will be deemed explainable if the complement to one of the sum of the RGE is significantly higher than a given bound (determined subjectively).

unit: The RGE function computes Rank Graduation Explainability for each model variable, for classification or prediction, and can statistically test whether overall explanation exceeds a set threshold or that of another model.
evidence: The RGE function can calculate the Rank Graduation Explainability (RGE) of each variable in the model, for classification (categorical response) or for prediction (continuous response). It can then conduct a statistical test to assess whether the overall explanation is significantly higher than a set threshold or to that of another model.

unit: The explainability scoring rubric rates a model's explainability score as Excellent (75%-90%), Good (70%-75%), Fair (60%-70%), Borderline (40%-60%) or Poor (0%-40%).
evidence: Once the outlined measurement metrics for RGE have been completed, it's important to score the explainability measure of your model(s). Here's a simple scoring rubric for explainability.

unit: RGE is a collection of statistics, one per feature, so values must be aggregated before mitigation; features are ranked by RGE and the number needed to reach a cumulative 50% is checked. A model is explainable if few features reach 50%, and not explainable if 50% is never reached or needs very many features.
evidence: Unlike RGA or RGR, RGE is not a single statistics but rather a collection of statistics, one for each feature in the model. Therefore, before making mitigation actions on RGE, it is necessary to aggregate the corresponding values. This can be done by examining the distribution of RGE values among the different features. For example, we can make a plot in which the feature variables are ordered in terms of their RGE values, from the highest to the lowest. Then check how many features are needed to reach a total RGE of 50%. If the 50% is reached with a small number of features, the model is explainable. If 50% is not reached after adding the RGE of all features, or if it is reached, but with a very large number of features, the model is not explainable.

unit: The 50% threshold and the meaning of a 'small number' of features are subjective and context specific: about three or four features for continuous monitoring, ten or twelve for descriptive contexts.
evidence: The threshold of 50% is purely indicative; a user can set a higher or a lower threshold, depending on the desired level of explainability. In terms of the number of explainable features, the definition of a "small number" again is subjective and context specific. If the context is that of continuous monitoring, "small" may mean three or four features; if the context is more descriptive, "small" may mean ten or twelve features.

unit: A model judged not explainable can be improved by simplifying it through model selection, removing features correlated with others without significantly reducing overall accuracy.
evidence: Make changes to the model: The machine learning model can be improved by means of model selection, which means trying to simplify the model by removing the features which are correlated with the others, without a significant reduction in the overall accuracy.

unit: Explainability can be improved by improving dataset quality: removing outliers or unrepresentative data and rebalancing training data via oversampling or undersampling.
evidence: Data quality can be improved by removing outlier data, or data that are not representative. Additionally, you can adjust the training data to better represent certain features (by means of oversampling or undersampling). This may lead to improved balance between the features.

unit: Explanations can be improved by increasing the data available, through augmentation with data from similar problems (meta analysis) or synthetic data generation.
evidence: Explanations can also be improved by increasing the available data in the dataset(s) and augmenting the available data with data from similar problems (meta analysis) or generating synthetic data.

unit: Explanations of ML models can be improved by increasing the data in the dataset(s), either by augmenting it with data from similar problems (meta analysis) or by generating synthetic data.
evidence: Increasing the amount of data: Explanations can also be improved by increasing the available data in the dataset(s) and augmenting the available data with data from similar problems (meta analysis) or generating synthetic data.

unit: The RGE (Rank Graduation Explainability) metric is normalized and can be interpreted as the percentage of model accuracy attributable to a feature, which is its advantage over standard measures such as Shapley values.
evidence: It's important to note that the advantage of our proposed metrics, RGE, with respect to standard measures such as Shapley values, is that it is normalized and interpretable as the percentage of model accuracy due to a feature.

unit: Because RGE is normalized and tied to accuracy, the results of mitigation actions can be evaluated directly as the added accuracy or explainability the changes bring to a model.
evidence: This allows us to evaluate the results of mitigation actions directly, in terms of the added accuracy/explainability brought to the model by the proposed changes.

unit: Shapley values cannot currently be used to evaluate mitigation actions directly, because their differential measurement is not normalized and not connected to predictive accuracy.
evidence: This is currently not possible with Shapley values as the differential measurement is not normalized and not connected to predictive accuracy.

unit: The Rank Graduation Explainability (RGE) measure quantifies explainability scores in ML models and can also be applied to mitigate and fix poor explainability measures.
evidence: To measure explainability values in an ML model, we introduced RGE, the Rank Graduation Explainability measure, an important metric which not only helps to measure explainability scores but can be applied in mitigating and fixing poor explainability measures in ML models.

unit: Responsible AI technologies are motivated by the aim of mitigating the risk that AI systems cause harms to individuals, organizations, and the environment.
evidence: The motivation to develop Responsible AI technologies aims at mitigating the risks that AI systems could cause harms on individuals, organizations, and the environment.

unit: Physical or psychological harms from AI systems are usually associated with and addressed under the heading of AI safety.
evidence: Such harms may be physical or psychological - which are usually associated and addressed under "AI safety."

unit: AI systems can also violate human rights, such as the right not to be discriminated against and the right to privacy.
evidence: We also have concerns about the violation of human rights, such as the right of not being discriminated against and the right to privacy, among others.

unit: Despite the large number of studies on fairness in machine learning, there is no universal measure for calculating fairness, and the literature considers several different notions of fairness.
evidence: Despite the vast number of studies on fairness, there are no universal measures to calculate it, and several notions of fairness have been considered in various literature.

unit: Teodorescu (2021) found that when more than one protected variable is considered in a classification problem, typical machine learning models do not satisfy more than one fairness criterion, which shows how hard it is to calculate fairness in decisions based on large databases such as credit scoring.
evidence: They show that when more than one protected variable is considered in a classification problem, the typical ML models do not satisfy more than one fairness criterion. This shows the difficulty of calculating fairness in decision-making processes using large databases such as credit scoring.

unit: Analysis of a huge credit scoring dataset shows that human input is needed in fairness decisions, especially when deciding trade-offs between fairness criteria.
evidence: The results found by analyzing a huge credit scoring dataset prove the need for human input in fairness decisions, especially when deciding trade-offs between fairness criteria.

unit: Horesh et al. (2020) propose an individual-based fairness approach that does not need a directly measurable protected variable, relying instead on an implicit idea of a potentially discriminatory variable, and that applies to a wide range of ML models.
evidence: The proposed approach in this paper has the following two general aspects: despite most fairness methods which rely on the presence of at least a protected variable, this proposed approach evaluates individual-based fairness using an implicit idea of a potentially discriminatory variable that does not have to be directly measurable. Secondly, it is applicable to a wide range of ML models.

unit: The paired consistency score defined by Horesh et al. measures the similarity of a model's predictions, for both regression and classification, for paired members.
evidence: In particular, they define a paired consistency score, which measures the similarity of a model's predictions, both for regression and classification, for paired members.

unit: Karimi et al. (2022) propose the FairMatch algorithm, which uses propensity score matching to pair similar and dissimilar individuals and introduces a new metric of individual fairness capturing similar treatment in probabilistic classifiers.
evidence: For example, Karimi et al. (2022) 41 propose the "FairMatch" algorithm which introduces a new approach to pairing similar and dissimilar individuals using a propensity score (PSM) matching method. They focus on individual fairness and propose a novel metric to evaluate individual fairness that captures the notion of similar treatment in probabilistic classifiers in a better way.

unit: Using four real-world datasets, Karimi et al. showed FairMatch to be superior to existing approaches, and the propensity score matching method also improves group-based fairness.
evidence: Using four real-world datasets, they show the superiority of FairMatch to the existing approaches. They also use the PSM method not only for matching the similar individuals but also to improve the group-based fairness.

unit: The requirement of fairness is related to the requirement of explainability, and Grabowicz et al. (2022) combine the two to obtain models that are both fair and interpretable.
evidence: It's important to note that the requirement of fairness is related to the requirement of explainability. A recent paper by Grabowicz et al. (2022) 42 combines the two requirements of fairness and explainability to obtain models which are both fair and interpretable.

unit: Conditional fairness holds when a machine learning model is considered fair because a given explanatory variable, such as leverage, has the same effect on the output across groups.
evidence: Using a notion of conditional fairness where a machine learning model is considered "fair" when a given explanatory variable, such as "leverage," has the same effect on the output.

unit: Marginal (unconditional) fairness requires that the model output, rather than its explanation, is the same for different population groups.
evidence: This is different from marginal (unconditional) fairness, which indicates that the output and not the explanation is the same for different population groups.

unit: Conditional fairness corresponds to individual fairness, while marginal fairness corresponds to group-based fairness.
evidence: Conditional fairness can be associated with "individual" fairness, whereas marginal fairness can be associated with group-based fairness.

unit: A Lorenz curve of the cumulative distribution of Shapley values of a variable, such as leverage, across countries provides a natural framework for assessing conditional fairness in credit scoring.
evidence: A natural framework to assess this type of fairness is by means of a Lorenz curve which represents the cumulative distribution of the Shapley values of a variable (such as leverage) for the different considered countries.

unit: Marginal fairness is easier to understand, but conditional fairness is more useful when structural characteristics in explanatory variables create certain biases.
evidence: Marginal fairness is easier to understand. On the other hand, conditional fairness is more useful when there are structural characteristics, corresponding to explanatory variables that make certain biases.

unit: Lower predictive accuracy for German companies, due to fewer balance sheets being deposited, does not necessarily indicate bias, and the Shapley values showed only a small bias, so the credit scoring model was conditionally fair.
evidence: For example, in the considered case, German companies are not required to deposit balance sheets, different from the others, and, therefore, the companies in the sample are much fewer. We thus expect a lower accuracy which, however, does not necessarily mean a bias. The Shapley values for leverage in the different countries are reported in Figure 5-2, and they indeed reveal a small bias.

unit: In the credit scoring case, predictive accuracy was similar across countries and years, indicating a high degree of marginal (group-based) fairness.
evidence: Figure 5-3 indicates a high degree of fairness, as predictive accuracies are similar and vary across the different years.

unit: The Rank Graduation Fairness (RGF) measure can be computed for classification (categorical response) and for prediction (continuous response) models using a Python function called check_fairness.
evidence: The RGF function can calculate the Rank Graduation Fairness (RGF) of a model, for classification (categorical response) or for prediction (continuous response).

unit: RGF, demonstrated on tabular data, can be extended to all data types including generative AI, provided that words or sentences associated with a protected variable are identified.
evidence: What presented for tabular data can be extended to all types of data, and it can cover generative AI as well. To this end, it is necessary to identify words or sentences that can be associated with a protected variable.

unit: The book's fairness scoring rubric rates a model's fairness score as Excellent (75%-90%), Good (70%-75%), Fair (60%-70%), Borderline (40%-60%) or Poor (0%-40%).
evidence: | What is the fairness score of your model(s)? | 75%-90%     | 70%-75% | 60%-70% | 40%-60%      | 0%-40% |

unit: Applying explainability methods, such as the RGE metrics, can help resolve fairness issues because a more explainable model pinpoints areas where the model may be failing on fairness.
evidence: Apply explainability methods: Using the RGE metrics discussed in the previous chapter to fix a poor explainable score in an AI model is one sure way to resolve fairness issues as a more explainable model pinpoints areas where the model could be defaulting on fairness.

unit: Resampling the dataset and oversampling underrepresented groups can resolve fairness issues by giving all groups adequate representation and balancing the data.
evidence: Make changes to the datasets: By resampling the dataset and adjusting the training data to represent more samples (oversampling) from underrepresented groups, fairness issues can be resolved as there'll be adequate representation of all groups in the dataset, which will balance it out.

unit: Creating synthetic data for underrepresented groups, guided by fairness test results, can improve dataset diversity and mitigate unfairness.
evidence: Leverage on synthetic data: You can also improve the diversity of the dataset by creating synthetic data for the underrepresented groups in the dataset, based on the fairness results when tested.

unit: Privacy in machine learning aims to preserve the privacy of individuals represented in datasets, using various techniques to safeguard sensitive data during ML development and deployment.
evidence: Privacy in machine learning aims to preserve the privacy of individuals represented in the datasets. It tends to employ and use different techniques to safeguard sensitive data during ML development and deployment.

unit: The NIST AI RMF recommends that an AI application be as independent as possible from individual observations, so that omitting information about one individual or a set of individuals has no relevant impact on the output.
evidence: To preserve privacy, the NIST AI RMF recommends an AI application should be as independent as possible from individual observations. In other words, omitting information about a single individual or about a given set of individuals should not have a relevant impact on the output.

unit: The degree of privacy and compliance with the privacy requirement can be measured by examining how much the model output depends on a given set of observations.
evidence: These considerations allow us to measure the degree of privacy and the degree of compliance with the privacy requirement, examining the dependence on the output on a given set of observations.

unit: Rank Graduation Privacy (RGP) extends the Rank Graduation Accuracy measure by comparing predictions from a model trained on all data with those from a model that excludes data points that must be "forgotten", reflecting the principle that personal data should be erased when no longer needed or upon request.
evidence: The Rank Graduation Accuracy (RGA) measurement can be extended to a Rank Graduation Privacy (RGP) measurement, comparing the predictions obtained with a model based on all data with those obtained from a model that excludes one or more data points which needs to be "forgotten" - an important principle in machine learning where personal data should be erased based on different circumstances, such as when personal data is no longer needed, or individuals have requested for the removal of their personal data.

unit: RGP is computed as the area between the dual Lorenz curve and the concordance curve, derived from the ranks of predictions made without the forgotten data, divided by its maximum possible value, the area between the dual Lorenz curve and the Lorenz curve.
evidence: The RGP metrics can be obtained by considering the area between the dual Lorenz curve and the concordance curve, derived from the ranks of the predictions obtained without the data to be forgotten, and dividing it by its maximum possible value - the area between the dual Lorenz curve and the Lorenz curve.

unit: Computing RGP involves four steps: fit a model on the full training set, predict on the test set, remove m observations and retrain on the remaining ones, then predict on the test set again and compare the two sets of predictions.
evidence:
Step 1: A machine learning model is fitted on the whole training set, including all n observations.

Step 2: The model fitted in step 1 is employed to obtain predicted values for the n observations in the test set.

Step 3: m observations (with m < N) are removed from the training set, and the model is trained on the remaining N-m observations.

Step 4: The model fitted at step 3 is employed to obtain predicted values for the n observations in the test set.

unit: The RGP measure is normalized: it equals 0 for irrelevant data and 1 for data of absolute importance, and otherwise lies between 0 and 1.
evidence: It is normalized: RGP=0 in the case of irrelevant data; RGP=1 for the case of data with absolute importance; in general, 0<RGP<1.

unit: A statistical test for RGP can check whether it passes a threshold for minimum privacy; a higher RGP means the data is more valuable, and a smaller p-value means the RGP is more significant relative to a given lower bound.
evidence: The higher the RGP, the higher the value of the data, and the smaller the p-value, the more significant the found RGP is with respect to a given lower bound.

unit: A high RGP value close to one, obtained when an observation is removed, means that removing that observation from the model does not affect its predictions.
evidence: Thus, removing the 10th observation leads to a high RGP, close to one, meaning that removing this observation from the model does not affect the predictions.

unit: In the example, the RGP-based statistical test for the 12th observation gave a very small p-value, so the null hypothesis was rejected and the prediction model was judged not compliant with the privacy criterion, as was the classification model.
evidence: The resulting p-value is equal to 1.65*10-08, which is a very small value. This leads us to reject the null hypothesis, which means that the ranks of the predictions by the reduced model are significantly different from those of the complete model, and the prediction model is not compliant to the privacy criterion, as it occurred for the classification model.

unit: Models trained on very little data find it difficult to comply with privacy requirements.
evidence: Both models use very little data, making it difficult to be compliant with the privacy requirements.

unit: Differential privacy protects data by adding noise or perturbations to training datasets, making it hard for attackers to identify personal information or individual records while still allowing aggregate statistics to be released.
evidence: Differential privacy: This introduces a mechanism of introducing "noise" or perturbations to the training datasets, making it difficult for any attacker to identify personal identifiable information or any individual record. This enables the release of aggregate statistics in ML models without compromising or revealing the privacy of the underlying data.

unit: Federated learning is a decentralized approach in which multiple devices train a shared model on local data and only model updates are combined into a global model, so personal data in each local dataset is not accessed.
evidence: Federated learning: Federated learning is a decentralized approach that enables multiple devices to collaborate on training a shared model without directly accessing their data. Each participant trains the model using their local data, and the model updates are combined to create a global model, without access to the personal data of each local dataset.

unit: Homomorphic encryption lets ML practitioners compute on encrypted data without decrypting it, so models can be trained and applied while sensitive user data stays protected throughout.
evidence: Homomorphic encryption: This employs a cryptographic encryption which doesn't require decryption of encrypted data before use and permits computation with encrypted data. This means that ML practitioners can build ML models trained and applied on encrypted data, which protects sensitive user data and information, ensuring they remain protected throughout the computation process.

unit: Adversarial training improves privacy and security by including adversarial examples in training so models become more robust against adversarial attacks and less susceptible to breaches.
evidence: It involves training ML models to be robust against adversarial attacks and malicious acts. This is carried out by including adversarial examples in the training process, enabling the models to be more resilient and less susceptible to privacy and security breaches.

unit: Secure multi-party computation lets multiple parties jointly compute over their inputs without revealing those inputs, which is useful for collaborating organizations that don't want to share sensitive data directly.
evidence: Secure MPC allows multiple parties to compute jointly over their inputs without revealing the individual inputs of the parties. This is a useful technique when you have several organizations or individuals working together on a particular ML task or project, but don't want to provide broad access to their individual data or share their sensitive data directly.

unit: ESG is a set of standards used to screen potential investments in a company based on how the company performs on environmental (E), social (S), and governance (G) dimensions.
evidence: ESG can be defined as a set of standards used to screen potential investments in a company on the basis of how the company performs in environment (E), social (S), and governance (G).

unit: ESG scores are very important for AI applications, and existing regulations reflect this importance.
evidence: ESG scores are very important for artificial intelligence applications, and this importance is reflected in the existing regulations.

unit: The EU AI Act recognizes AI's environmental benefits across industries and allows supervisors to consider the estimated energy consumption of training when a general purpose AI model poses a systemic risk.
evidence: For example, the EU AI Act, while acknowledging that AI contributes to a wide range of environmental benefits "across the entire spectrum of industries and social activities," also states that "when a general purpose AI model poses a systemic risk, supervisors may consider the estimated energy consumption of training AI models."

unit: The United Nations AI Advisory Board's interim report says a key measure of success is the extent to which AI technologies help achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
evidence: At a higher level, the United Nations AI Advisory Board states, at the beginning of its interim report (article 4), that "a key measure of our success is the extent to which AI technologies help achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)."

unit: Because ESG factors are highly related to the SDGs, AI applications that take ESG factors into account may help achieve the SDGs.
evidence: Environmental, social, and governance factors are highly related to all 16 SDG goals so that, if AI applications take into account ESG factors, they may help to achieve SDG goals as well.

unit: High-impact industrial sectors such as energy and fashion may benefit from including ESG criteria in their key performance indicators, because better ESG scores make them more attractive to investors and consumers who see them as more sustainable long term.
evidence: Industrial sectors or verticals which have a high impact on the environment, such as energy and fashion, to name a few, may strongly benefit from the inclusion of ESG criteria in their key performance indicators. Better ESG scores can make companies in these sectors more attractive for investors and consumers, as they are perceived to be more sustainable in the long run.

unit: Unlike traditional financial indicators, ESG criteria aim to enhance returns while also promoting positive social and environmental outcomes. Incorporating them into investment decisions is called sustainable finance, which is meant to increase long-term investment in sustainable economic activities and projects.
evidence: From a financial perspective, contrary to more traditional financial indicators, the criteria for ESG aims at enhancing returns while simultaneously promoting positive social and environmental outcomes. 51 The incorporation of such standards in the investment decision-making process is defined as "sustainable finance," and it is meant to increase long-term investments in sustainable economic activities and projects.

unit: Because authorities have issued little or no ESG regulation, rating agencies choose their own methodologies for assessing corporate sustainability, and the reasons behind scores from platforms like Refinitiv or Bloomberg may be hard to interpret.
evidence: Despite the unstoppable growth ESG has experienced since the Great Recession in 2008, authorities have come up with little or no regulation on the matter, leaving rating agencies free to decide their own methodology for the assessment of a corporate's sustainability performance. In a similar context, the interpretation of ESG scores as provided by major financial platforms - such as Refinitiv or Bloomberg - becomes challenging, as the reasons behind the scores may not be clearly interpretable.

unit: A growing number of firms engage in greenwashing, misleading stakeholders about their sustainable performance.
evidence: Indeed, more and more firms engage in "greenwashing" behaviors, ultimately misleading stakeholders about their sustainable performance.

unit: The environmental (E) dimension of ESG refers to a company's efforts on climate change mitigation and adoption, such as limiting harmful pollutants and chemicals or reducing greenhouse emissions. It has been the most popular ESG item in both firm implementation and rating agency evaluation.
evidence: E, which stands for "environment," typically refers to a company's effort on climate change mitigation and adoption. It may account for a company's limitation on the usage of harmful pollutants and chemicals or to a company's active engagement in the reduction of greenhouse emission. 55 Among the three ESG items, environment (E) has always been the most popular one, both in terms of implementation on the firms' side and in terms of evaluation by rating agencies.

unit: The social (S) dimension of ESG covers company policies on inequality, inclusiveness, labor relations and human rights, and may also assess business relationships, employee health and safety, and working conditions.
evidence: S, which represents "social criteria," usually refers to the policies promoted by a company on the matter of inequality, inclusiveness, labor relation, and human rights issues. A company's business relationships alongside employees' health and safety and working conditions may be evaluated as well.

unit: The governance (G) dimension of ESG may account for conflicts of interest in choosing board members and for the percentage of female board members or gender diversity in the company.
evidence: G, representing "governance," may account for the presence of conflict of interest in the choice of board members, the percentage of female board members, or, in general, the percentage of gender diversity in a company.

unit: Higher social (S) and governance (G) scores significantly reduce a firm's five-year default probability: a 10% increase lowers it by about 0.5% and 0.9% respectively, while a 10% increase in the total ESG score raises it by about 0.7%.
evidence: More precisely, an increase by 10% in either social (S) or governance (G) scores leads to a decrease of the default probability by about 0.5 and 0.9%, respectively. These effects are counterbalanced by the opposite effect of the total ESG score, whose 10% increase leads to an increase of the default probability of about 0.7%.

unit: Summing the three linear coefficients, the net effect of a 10% increase in E, S, and G is a decrease in default probability of about 0.7%, roughly a 16% decrease relative to the average PD of about 4.30.
evidence: However, summing up the three linear coefficients, we see that the overall effect is negative, with a decrease in the default probability of about 0.7% when all of E, S, and G increase by 10%. If we compare the decrease in PD with the average PD of about 4.30, as seen in the previous section, we roughly obtain a 16% decrease of the PD, implied by ESG factors.

unit: Firms can reduce their probability of default by increasing their investment in social (S) and governance (G) factors.
evidence: This result demonstrates that by enhancing the share of ESG investment in social (S) and governance(G), firms can reduce the probability of default.

unit: The percentage of women on a company's Board is negatively correlated with default probability, so more women on the Board means lower default risk.
evidence: The authors also show that the percentage of women on Board is negatively correlated with the default probability; thus, the more women there are on the Board, the lower the risk of default.

unit: More women on the Board improve corporate outcomes by increasing dialogue among board members, improving decision-making quality, and favoring innovative and competitive strategies.
evidence: More women in the Board increase dialogue among board members, improve the quality of decision-making process, and favor the implementation of innovative and competitive business strategies, with a positive effect on corporate outcomes.

unit: The number of female directors is positively and significantly correlated with the presence of CSR committees, which supports sustainability financially, socially, and in governance.
evidence: This conclusion is reinforced by a found positive and significant correlation between the number of female directors and the presence of CSR committees, in line with the extant literature. This favors sustainability, not only from a financial viewpoint but also from a social and governance perspective.

unit: E, S, and G indicators can be used to assess the sustainability of a company, including one that produces, deploys, or uses AI applications.
evidence: More generally, environment (E), social (S), and governance (G) indicators can be used to assess the sustainability of a company and of a company that produces, deploys, or uses artificial intelligence applications.

unit: The Rank Graduation Explainability (RGE) measure can assess the relevance of ESG factors and thereby model sustainability; applied to E, S, and G scores as explanatory variables, it yields the Rank Graduation Sustainability (RGS) measure, which has the same properties as RGE.
evidence: The Rank Graduation Explainability (RGE) measure can be employed to assess the relevance of ESG factors, thereby measuring model sustainability. We can consider E, S, and G scores as explanatory variables and calculate their explainability as we did in Chapter 4.

unit: The sustainability of an ML model depends heavily on its ability to have a positive impact on society, and AI can both help (e.g., healthcare diagnosis, drug discovery) and harm society through risks such as bias, hallucinations, privacy violations and security threats.
evidence: The sustainability of an ML model is highly dependent on its ability to have a positive impact on society. 60 In some areas, such as healthcare, AI is helping to provide more accurate medical diagnosis, driving drug discovery, assisting with higher-precision surgeries, developing personalized treatment plans, and so on.

unit: To address AI's societal risks, organizations should follow the book's recommendations and ensure datasets are diverse and inclusive and that ML design teams are made up of diverse groups of people.
evidence: To navigate these issues, aligning to the various recommendations in this book will help to resolve most of the challenges AI systems pose to society. Also, ensuring datasets are diverse and inclusive, and ML development/design teams are made up of diverse groups of people, will assist with this issue.

unit: For AI systems to be economically sustainable, their benefits must outweigh costs and they must return value for money; some businesses have turned off generative AI pilots because of high investment with little ROI.
evidence: With the recent surge of generative AI, experts and business executives are beginning to question the value of generative AI as it demands high investment running into millions of dollars, with very little turnover, profit, or return on investment (ROI). While it might be early days to conclude on the overall value of generative AI to businesses given it's only been around for roughly two years, a few businesses have turned off their generative AI pilots and campaigns as they haven't seen value for money. For AI systems to be sustainable and economically viable, it's crucial they return value for money.

unit: Organizations should create new job opportunities, ensure workers have the skills to navigate AI disruption, and design AI to augment rather than replace human capabilities to achieve economic sustainability.
evidence: Although the forecasted number of impacted jobs by AI might be quite speculative and yet to be proven, it's important efforts are made by organizations to ensure new job opportunities are created and workers have the necessary skills to navigate this disruptive technical revolution. To ensure AI systems achieve economic sustainability, it's important AI design includes the augmentation of human capabilities and not the replacement of them.

unit: AI's environmental impact is high because large data centers and GPUs supporting billions of parameters, especially for foundation models, consume large amounts of energy.
evidence: However, the negative impact AI systems have on the environment is too high to ignore, largely due to the high amount of computing resources required to run these machines. From very large data centers to large GPUs (Graphics Processing Units) to support the billions of parameters needed for AI - particularly large-scale or foundation models - the energy consumption derived from these systems is quite high and concerning.

unit: Reducing AI's carbon footprint promotes energy-efficient hardware and greener algorithms, and building smaller, more efficient AI models can help reduce environmental impact.
evidence: Reducing the carbon footprint of AI machines will lead to the promotion of more energy-efficient hardware and more greener algorithms. Work is being done in this area by various AI start-ups looking for alternative ways to develop AI chips and GPUs. Building smaller and more efficient AI models could also help to combat this issue.

unit: The chapter's sustainability scoring rubric rates models as Excellent (75%-90%), Good (70%-75%), Fair (60%-70%), Borderline (40%-60%) or Poor (0%-40%).
evidence: | What is the sustainability score of your model(s)? | 75%-90%     | 70%-75% | 60%-70% | 40%-60%      | 0%-40% |
