section_path: Introduction to the Problems and Opportunities

unit: Because technological, environmental, demographic and socioeconomic disruption challenges societies, teaching more relevant content is no longer sufficient; innovation ecosystems that harness disruption are needed, and transformative learning within them can shift mindsets toward meaningful change and a more sustainable, humane world.
evidence: It is no longer sufficient to 'teach' more relevant content. (Innovation) Ecosystems that harness disruption for the benefit of people and organizations are needed. Transformative learning as part of an innovation eco-system is able to transform mindsets to empower people and organizations to embrace radical but meaningful change and create a more sustainable world and more humane societies.

unit: Technologies should be deployed in service of a purpose: creating an inclusive, value-adding society, helping people continuously learn, and developing future competencies so people can reinvent themselves rather than being tied to an obsolete profession.
evidence: While technologies available today can be marvellous tools, they should be deployed to serve the purpose: create a value adding, impactful and inclusive society; support people in how to learn to continuously learn; develop the competencies of the future, so that people can reinvent themselves at any time and are not limited to a no longer existing profession they were trained for.

unit: The aim of PRME's principle three is to produce responsible, learning and caring individuals who both know what should be done and are able to achieve it.

unit: The COVID-19 pandemic made continuity of higher education a major challenge and, by raising the question of how to make higher education available to all classes, pushed HEIs toward greater openness and digital transformation and strengthened the case for sustainability, inclusivity, equity and responsible management education.
evidence: The biggest question was how we make higher education available for all, across classes in the society. It was this burning question which pushed HEIs towards greater openness and digital transformation. Pandemic also made a strong case for discussions on sustainability, inclusivity and equity in education and advocated for the expansion of responsible management education.

unit: MOOCs have gained prominence as a way to improve access to higher education, reduce inadequacies in education systems and democratize higher education, and they are a preferred tool for building a sustainability mindset and teaching social responsibility, inclusion, empathy and responsible management.

MOOCS have also become the preferred tool for creating sustainability mindset and sharing knowledge on social responsibility, inclusion, empathy and responsible management education.

unit: The Principles of Responsible Management Education (PRME), in place since 2007, aim to stimulate thinking about responsibility and sustainability in business schools so that current and future leaders gain the skills and knowledge to implement the 17 Sustainable Development Goals.
evidence: Their aim is to stimulate the thinking of responsibility and sustainability in business and management schools around the world so that current and future business leaders will acquire the necessary skills and knowledge to implement the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

unit: The Trustworthy AI Maturity Model (TAIMM) is a lifecycle-based evaluation framework designed to support the development of ethically aligned and legally compliant AI systems.
evidence: This paper introduces the Trustworthy AI Maturity Model (TAIMM), a lifecycle-based evaluation framework designed to support the development of ethically aligned and legally compliant Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems.

unit: Current AI governance approaches suffer from an implementation gap: they often endorse high-level ethical principles but lack tools for operationalising them in practice, which TAIMM is meant to address.
evidence: TAIMM responds to the implementation gap in current AI governance approaches, which often endorse high-level ethical principles but lack tools for operationalising them in practice.

unit: TAIMM targets high-risk systems under the EU AI Act, mapping the Act's recitals to the seven principles of Trustworthy AI and integrating them into a governance framework grounded in established System Development lifecycle models.
evidence: Focusing on highrisk systems under the European Union's AI Act, the model maps the Act's recitals to the seven principles of Trustworthy AI and integrates them into a structured governance framework grounded in established System Development lifecycle models.

unit: Unlike general AI management standards such as ISO 42001, TAIMM is a maturity-oriented diagnostic tool tailored to the AI lifecycle.
evidence: Unlike general AI management standards such as ISO 42001, TAIMM provides a maturity-oriented diagnostic tool tailored to the AI lifecycle.

unit: TAIMM includes three stage-specific questionnaires covering design, development, and operation, with each item explicitly labelled with its corresponding ethical principle.
evidence: The framework includes three stage-specific questionnaires covering design, development, and operation each item explicitly labelled with its corresponding ethical principle.

unit: Labelling items by ethical principle enables actionable self-assessment and quantitative analysis of ethical coverage, revealing disparities in emphasis and underrepresented principles.
evidence: This approach enables both actionable self-assessment and quantitative analysis of ethical coverage, revealing disparities in emphasis and highlighting underrepresented principles.

unit: AI-specific maturity models remain fragmented and underdeveloped, particularly regarding trustworthiness and compliance under emerging legal frameworks, even though maturity models have long been used to assess organisational capabilities in fields like software engineering and cybersecurity.
evidence: Yet, AI-specific maturity models remain fragmented and underdeveloped, particularly with respect to trustworthiness and compliance in the context of emerging legal frameworks (Akbarighatar et al., 2023).

evidence: The former introduces a risk-based legal framework for high-risk AI systems, while the latter provides a process-based AI management system akin to ISO 9001 (International Organization for Standardization, 2015).

unit: The EU AI Act has been criticised for lacking implementation clarity in fast-moving, ambiguous technological contexts. ISO 42001 has been criticised for limited transparency to external stakeholders and for requiring complexity, knowledge and governance structures that organisations may lack.
evidence: However, both have been criticised: the EU AI Act for its lack of implementation clarity in fast-moving and ambiguous technological contexts (Korshenko, 2024; Ruschemeier, 2023), and ISO 42001 for a number of reasons including a lack of transparency to external stakeholders (Thiers & Harned, 2024) and the complexity and level of knowledge or governance structures required to correctly implement high level frameworks like ISO 42001 may not always exist within organisations causing issues for effective implementation (Dudley, 2024; Suredranath, 2025).

unit: The Trustworthy AI Maturity Model (TAIMM) integrates the ethical guidance of the Trustworthy AI principles with the EU AI Act's regulatory requirements, and operationalises standards like ISO 42001 through a system-level, lifecycle-based evaluation framework.
evidence: TAIMM integrates the ethical guidance of the Trustworthy AI principles with the regulatory requirements of the EU AI Act. TAIMM operationalises standards like ISO 42001 by providing a system-level, lifecycle-based evaluation framework aligned with AI requirements originating in the AI Act.

unit: TAIMM helps organisations assess, benchmark and improve their readiness for ethically aligned and legally compliant AI development.
evidence: It supports organisations in assessing, benchmarking, and improving their readiness for ethically aligned and legally compliant AI development.

unit: TAIMM is built by mapping the EU AI Act recitals to the seven Trustworthy AI principles and aligning them with Laato et al.'s AI governance framework, producing a principle-labelled questionnaire for each of the design, development and operation phases that enables quantifiable evaluation of ethical coverage.
evidence: Our method addresses the practical implementation gap by mapping the recitals of the EU AI Act to the seven principles of Trustworthy AI and aligning them with an established AI governance framework by Laato et al. (2022). This results in a structured, principle-labelled questionnaire for each of the three key lifecycle phases design, development, and operation enabling quantifiable evaluation of ethical coverage across the AI system lifecycle.

unit: Terminology around AI trustworthiness is vague and overlapping, so different terms such as 'responsible AI' are used for similar concepts, methods, and tools, which produces confusing results.
evidence: The terminology of trustworthiness in AI is quite vague, ambiguous, and sometimes overlapping terms are used for various characteristics of trustworthiness, which leads to confusing results; for example, another term that is commonly used refers to 'responsible AI', which addresses similar concepts, methods, and tools (Mentzas et al., 2024).

unit: The TAIMM paper defines trustworthy AI using the European Commission's Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI and the Assessment List for Trustworthy AI (ALTAI), which give the normative foundation for evaluating AI systems.
evidence: In this paper we use the term trustworthy AI as it is detailed in the European Commission's Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI (European Commission High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, 2019) and the Assessment List for Trustworthy AI (ALTAI) (Hleg, 2020), which provide the normative foundation for evaluating AI systems.

unit: Although the trustworthy AI principles are referenced in the EU AI Act, they are non-binding and their operationalisation in practice remains inconsistent.
evidence: Though referenced in the EU AI Act (European Union, 2024), these principles are non-binding, and their operationalisation remains inconsistent in practice.

unit: The human agency and oversight principle holds that AI should facilitate rather than replace human decision-making, preserving human autonomy and enabling oversight through human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop control, especially in high-stakes contexts.
evidence: AI should act as a facilitator of human decision-making, not a substitute. Systems must be designed to preserve human autonomy and ensure oversight remains possible at all times. This includes enabling mechanisms such as human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop control, which allow for meaningful human intervention, particularly in high-stakes or safety-critical contexts.

unit: Technical robustness and safety requires AI systems to be reliable and accurate under normal conditions and capable of performing under unforeseen or adversarial scenarios, with safety mechanisms such as fallback plans.
evidence: Robustness refers not only to the reliability and accuracy of the system under standard conditions but also to its capacity to perform under unforeseen or adversarial scenarios. Safety mechanisms, including fallback plans, should be in place to address potential failures or harm arising from system behaviour.

unit: The transparency principle requires AI systems to be explainable in a way suited to the stakeholder, with clarity about purpose, data sources, decision logic, and limitations, and decisions contestable where possible.
evidence: Systems should be explainable in a way that is appropriate to the stakeholder, whether a developer, regulator, or end-user. This includes clarity about the system's purpose, data sources, decision-making logic, and limitations. Where possible, decisions should be contestable.

unit: The fairness principle extends beyond technical debiasing to include inclusive design, stakeholder participation, and accessibility and equity in system inputs and outcomes.
evidence: Fairness extends beyond technical debiasing to include inclusive design practices and stakeholder participation. Accessibility and equity are essential considerations in both system inputs and outcomes.

unit: Most organisations struggle to turn abstract trustworthy AI values into technical or organisational procedures, creating a need for frameworks that embed ethical principles into AI lifecycle processes, especially for high-risk applications.
evidence: Despite broad endorsement, most organisations struggle to translate these abstract values into technical or organisational procedures. This gap highlights the need for frameworks that embed ethical principles directly into AI lifecycle processes, particularly for high-risk applications.

unit: ISO 42001 has been criticised for lacking specifications to operationalise ethical AI principles, and for organisations lacking the knowledge to implement it correctly.
evidence: ISO 42001, for instance, has been criticised for lacking specifications to operationalise ethical AI principles, with concerns around the lack of knowledge to correctly implement the standards within organisations (Dudley, 2024).

unit: ISO 42001 gives only high-level guidance with limited technical depth for implementation, especially in specific regulatory or organisational contexts.
evidence: It provides high-level guidance but limited technical depth for implementation, especially within specific regulatory or organisational contexts (Simonetta & Paoletti, 2024).

unit: ISO 42001 lacks controls for large language model risks such as hallucination and real-time compliance oversight, limiting its effectiveness in high-risk AI contexts.
evidence: One such context where it lacks explicit provisions is for large language models (LLM's) where it fails to provide controls for risks such as content hallucination and real-time compliance oversight, limiting its effectiveness in high-risk AI contexts (McIntosh et al., 2024).

unit: The EU AI Act is legally binding for high-risk systems but has been described as too abstract to effectively guide implementation workflows.
evidence: Similarly, the EU AI Act, while legally binding for high-risk systems, has been described as too abstract to guide implementation workflows effectively (Korshenko, 2024).

unit: Fairness is the most mature domain of AI ethics evaluation, with measurable metrics and tooling, whereas principles such as societal well-being or accountability remain difficult to assess systematically.
evidence: Of these, fairness is the most mature domain, with measurable metrics and tooling. However, many other principles such as societal well-being or accountability remain difficult to assess systematically (McCormack & Bendechache, 2024b).

unit: Yajima et al. propose a risk assessment framework aligned with ISO 31000 and ISO 42001 that evaluates AI across ethics, quality and security, but it focuses on risk assessment and cannot diagnose organisational readiness or Trustworthy AI implementation maturity across the lifecycle.
evidence:
Yajima et al. (2024) propose a comprehensive risk assessment framework aligned with ISO 31000 and ISO 42001, which evaluates AI systems across ethics, quality, and security dimensions, offering an operational approach to compliance for high-risk systems. However, while their framework offers a structured method for risk identification and prioritisation aligned with ISO 42001, it remains primarily focused on risk assessment rather than broader governance or maturity evaluation.
Their approach does not provide a mechanism for assessing the organisational or procedural readiness of AI providers across the full system lifecycle, nor does it support continuous ethical benchmarking or principle-level coverage analysis.
As such, it lacks the capacity to function as a diagnostic tool for Trustworthy AI implementation maturity.

unit: Prokopchina's Measuring Artificial Intelligence (MAI) concept combines measurement science and Bayesian approaches for traceability and trust in AI outputs, but lacks practical tools for lifecycle governance or maturity assessment.
evidence: Prokopchina (2024) introduces the concept of Measuring Artificial Intelligence (MAI), integrating measurement science and Bayesian approaches to ensure traceability and trust in AI outputs. While valuable in addressing data quality and uncertainty, this approach lacks practical tools for lifecycle governance or maturity assessment across organisational settings, which limits its usability for operationalising broader AI ethics and legal compliance.

unit: Laato et al. (2022) propose a lifecycle-based AI governance model with three stages: System Design, System Development, and System Operation, linking governance concerns to tasks like data validation, model explanation, and ongoing monitoring.
evidence: Recent work by Laato et al. (2022) introduces a lifecycle-based AI governance model aligned to three key stages: System Design, System Development, and System Operation. This structure links governance concerns to practical system-building tasks such as data validation, model explanation, and ongoing monitoring.

evidence: These approaches emphasise ethical integration from the outset, supporting long-term accountability and public trust. Yet, these tools and frameworks lack cohesive maturity assessments and do not include mechanisms to benchmark organisational progress.

unit: TAIMM is a stage-based framework that links ethical principles and regulatory requirements to lifecycle stages, embedding a maturity-based diagnostic system aligned to Trustworthy AI principles and the EU AI Act for high-risk AI systems.
evidence: TAIMM differs from existing standards by embedding a maturity-based diagnostic system aligned to both the Trustworthy AI principles and the EU AI Act, specifically for high-risk AI systems.

unit: The EU AI Act uses a tiered, risk-based classification, and high-risk AI systems, which significantly affect health, safety or fundamental rights, face the strictest obligations, including transparency, data governance, human oversight and post-market monitoring.
evidence: The EU AI Act introduces a tiered, risk-based classification scheme to regulate AI applications. High-risk AI systems those with significant implications for health, safety, or fundamental rights are subject to the strictest governance obligations, including transparency, data governance, human oversight, and post-market monitoring (European Union, 2024).
section_path: 2.3. AI lifecycle models and maturity frameworks

unit: Under the EU AI Act, responsibility is shared among providers, deployers, importers and distributors, with providers bearing the most obligations; education systems are among those classed as high-risk.
evidence: Responsibility under the Act is distributed across roles including providers, deployers, importers, and distributors, with providers bearing the most extensive obligations. Systems are classified as high-risk based on both context and impact. These include biometric identification, law enforcement, education, critical infrastructure, and migration/border control systems.
section_path: 2.3. AI lifecycle models and maturity frameworks

unit: The Trustworthy AI Maturity Model (TAIMM) is a structured, lifecycle-based framework that integrates the ethical guidance of the EU HLEG Trustworthy AI principles with the regulatory requirements of the EU AI Act.
evidence: This paper proposes the Trustworthy AI Maturity Model (TAIMM): a structured, lifecycle-based framework that integrates the ethical guidance of the Trustworthy AI principles with the regulatory requirements of the EU AI Act.

unit: TAIMM was designed to address gaps in existing governance instruments, namely the lack of actionable tools for operationalising ethics and assessing maturity across AI system lifecycles.
evidence: Our methodology was designed to address identified gaps in existing governance instruments namely, the lack of actionable tools for operationalising ethics and assessing maturity across AI system lifecycles.

unit: TAIMM structures its questionnaires around the three lifecycle phases of Laato et al. (2022): System Design, System Development, and System Operation, chosen because that framework builds on established system lifecycle frameworks.
evidence: To ensure a cohesive, formal approach to AI governance, we chose the framework from Laato et al. (2022), which built upon existing established system lifecycle frameworks in the literature. Using the requirements detailed in the recitals of the EU AI Act, we developed detailed questionnaires which we mapped to different phases of AI development, using Laato et al.'s 2022 three tiered phases, System Design, System Development, and System Operation.

unit: Each TAIMM questionnaire item is mapped to the relevant Trustworthy AI principle(s), enabling quantitative analysis of a system's trustworthiness.
evidence: We ensured each of the actionable questions were also mapped to the relevant Trustworthy AI principle(s) to enable a quantitative analysis of Trustworthy AI for that system.

unit: TAIMM uses mapping tables aligning EU AI Act recital requirements with lifecycle stages, making it easy for AI providers to identify compliance areas.
evidence: We did this by creating mapping tables to align specific requirements from the AI Act recitals, with the identified system lifecycle stages, facilitating easy identification of compliance areas for AI providers.

unit: TAIMM's questionnaires were designed to be manageable for providers with limited resources, and the process was documented to make the framework repeatable for guiding implementation.
evidence: We designed manageable questionnaires suitable for providers with limited resources and documented our entire process to provide a coherent, repeatable framework for guiding actionable implementation.

unit: Counting questionnaire items per principle in each lifecycle phase shows which Trustworthy AI principles are emphasised at each stage, validating the questionnaire structure and indicating where ethical attention is embedded in the lifecycle.
evidence: We then calculated how many questions corresponded to each principle within the System Design, System Development, and System Operation phases. This enabled us to visualise the distribution and identify which principles are emphasised at each stage. This analytical layer provided both validation for our questionnaire structure and insights into where ethical attention is most frequently embedded in the lifecycle, offering a basis for future refinement of AI governance tools.

unit: The EU AI Act states that AI systems should be designed to align with ethical principles of trustworthiness, human agency, technical robustness, transparency, fairness, privacy, and societal well-being, serving people while minimising harm, bias, and environmental impact.
evidence: The EU AI Act states that AI systems should be designed to align with ethical principles ensuring trustworthiness, human agency, technical robustness, transparency, fairness, privacy, and societal well-being, serving people while minimising harm, bias, and environmental impact.

unit: The EU AI Act requires that AI systems be designed and deployed with sufficient human oversight throughout their lifecycle in order to ensure ethical compliance.
evidence: The EU AI Act emphasises that AI systems must be designed and deployed with sufficient human oversight throughout their lifecycle to ensure ethical compliance (48).

unit: Under the EU AI Act, people must be told when they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the context of use.
evidence: Natural persons must be informed when they are interacting with an AI system unless this is obvious from the context of use (70).

unit: AI systems should allow deployers to understand outputs, assess functionality, and recognise the system's strengths and limitations, which supports informed human control.
evidence: Systems should enable deployers to understand system outputs, assess functionality, and recognise strengths and limitations, thereby supporting informed human control (47).

unit: Providers of high-risk AI systems must put post-market monitoring in place to improve performance and address emerging risks, especially for systems that keep learning after deployment, and must report serious incidents to the relevant authorities.
evidence: For highrisk AI systems, providers must implement post-market monitoring mechanisms to improve system performance and address emerging risks, particularly where systems continue learning after deployment, and must report serious incidents to relevant authorities (155).

unit: AI systems must be designed and used as tools that serve people, uphold human dignity and personal autonomy, and permit appropriate human control and supervision.
evidence: Overall, AI systems must be designed and used as tools that serve people, uphold human dignity and personal autonomy, and allow for appropriate human control and supervision (27).

unit: The EU AI Act's accountability requirements mandate that high-risk AI systems include comprehensive technical documentation covering system characteristics, capabilities, limitations, data and model processes, and risk management measures, and support automatic event logging across their lifecycle for traceability and auditability.
evidence: Accountability requirements mandate that high-risk AI systems include comprehensive technical documentation covering system characteristics, capabilities, limitations, data and model processes, and risk management measures. Systems must also support automatic logging of events throughout their lifecycle to enable traceability and auditability (46).

unit: High-risk AI systems must undergo conformity assessments under applicable EU harmonisation legislation before market placement or deployment, and providers must establish processes for reporting, investigating and addressing incidents as part of post-market monitoring.
evidence: Prior to market placement or deployment, high-risk AI systems must undergo conformity assessments in accordance with applicable EU harmonisation legislation to ensure regulatory compliance (62-63). Providers must further establish clear processes for reporting, investigating, and addressing incidents as part of post-market monitoring obligations (78).

unit: The Laato et al. ML governance framework, drawn from industry interviews, aligns AI governance themes to three lifecycle stages: design, development, and operation, each with specific activities and thematic concerns.
evidence: Drawing on the study ''AI Governance in the System Development Life Cycle: Insights on Responsible Machine Learning Engineering'' by Laato et al. we utilised their framework, detailed in Fig. 2, which aligns AI governance concepts and themes they gathered from industry interviews to three core stages of the AI lifecycle, design, development, and operation.

unit: In Laato et al.'s System Design stage, the themes are the business case (suitability of ML and project-level requirements), data resources (availability, usability and data ethics), and the external environment (IT infrastructure, technical tools and regulatory compliance).
evidence: In the System Design phase, the first theme is the business case, which includes evaluating the suitability of machine learning for the problem at hand and identifying project-level requirements. The second theme is data resources, assessing the availability and usability of data, as well as ethical considerations surrounding its use.

unit: In Laato et al.'s framework, System Development covers data development (versioning and validation) and model development (model versions, algorithmic choices, parameter weights), while System Operation adds model explanation (interpretation and XAI tools) and automated monitoring (bias and anomaly detection). System testing spans both development and operation.
evidence: Data development involves versioning and validation processes. Model development includes managing model versions, specifying algorithmic choices, and setting parameter weights. System testing which includes manual reviews, the use of test datasets, and considerations related to the operational environment is included in both the System Development and the System Operation phases. In addition to system testing, the System Operation phase includes model explanation, and automated monitoring.

unit: TAIMM maps EU AI Act recitals to the seven Trustworthy AI principles and to the three lifecycle stages of Laato et al., which translates abstract ethical principles into practical compliance and governance processes.
evidence: The integration of the recitals and Trustworthy AI principles into this governance framework allowed for a robust, actionable framework to translate abstract ethical principles into practical compliance and governance processes.

unit: Manual questionnaire-based assessment is currently the most commonly used method for evaluating Trustworthy AI, even though some automated and semi-automated methods exist.
evidence: Although some automated and semi-automated methods to evaluate systems for Trustworthy AI exist, currently manual questionnaire-based assessment is the most commonly used evaluation method (McCormack & Bendechache, 2024a).

unit: The Asimovian Principles, inspired by Isaac Asimov and originally formulated for robotics, comprise three laws: a robot may not harm humans or allow harm through inaction, must obey human orders unless they conflict with the First Law, and must protect its own existence unless this conflicts with the first two laws.

First Law: A robot may not injure a human being, or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.

unit: Generative AI in higher education has introduced a range of ethical challenges that significantly affect learning outcomes, pedagogies, and assessments.
evidence: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has introduced a spectrum of ethical challenges, significantly impacting learning outcomes, pedagogies, and assessments.

unit: Students and teachers at a Hong Kong research university raised concerns about academic integrity, fairness, equity, privacy and data security, including invisible labour from ambiguous policies, uneven enforcement, detection loopholes, unequal access to advanced tools, and cognitive and developmental harms from overreliance on GenAI.
evidence: The findings reveal general concerns about academic integrity, fairness, equity, privacy, and data security, including specifically the invisible labour in dealing with ambiguous policies, uneven enforcement strategies, loopholes to avoid detection, disparities in access to state-of-the-art tools, and the cognitive and other developmental impacts due to overreliance on GenAI tools.

unit: Institutional ambiguity in AI policy enabled experimentation and the appearance of progress, but risked placing the blame for failure on individual teachers and students.
evidence: Institutional ambiguity in policy supported experimentation and the appearance of progress, but risked individualising failure on teachers and students.

unit: University leaders, teaching development centres, and teachers should provide clearer messaging, adaptive policies and guidelines with ongoing student and teacher participation, digital libraries of toolkits and case studies, early "failure experiences", and exposure to authentic real-world applications to build awareness of GenAI's limitations.
evidence: Some actionable insights for university leaders and policymakers, teaching development centres, and individual teachers and programme coordinators include clearer messaging, the need for adaptive policies and guidelines with ongoing student and teacher participation, availability of digital libraries of toolkits, case studies and other resources, building in early "failure experiences", and exposing students to authentic real-world applications and encounters to cultivate awareness on the limitations of GenAI.

unit: Policy responses to GenAI must be sensitive to context and practicality, and require on-the-ground experimentation and care by teachers.
evidence: Ultimately, policy responses need to be both contextually and pragmatically sensitive, requiring on-the-ground experimentation and care by teachers.

unit: The policy trajectories concept (Ball) is used to analyse how material contexts and discursive constructions interconnect in the framing, interpretation, enactment, and resistance of AI policies and their absence.
evidence: Through the concept of policy trajectories (Ball, 1993; Ball et al., 2012), the research analyses the interconnections between material contexts and discursive constructions in how AI policies (and their absence) are framed, interpreted, enacted, and resisted.

unit: Widespread use of generative AI has reshaped student and teacher attitudes and behaviour, raising concerns about academic integrity, fairness, equity, algorithmic bias, and overdependence that undermines institutions' desired graduate outcomes.
evidence: The resulting wide usage has reconfigured the attitudes and behaviour of students and teachers, prompting numerous concerns around academic integrity, fairness, equity, algorithmic bias, and problems of overdependence that undermine institutions' desired outcomes for graduates.

unit: A Purdue University case study found that before formal institutional guidance, faculty responses to GenAI varied widely; even in a technology-focused department, under a third of syllabi mentioned LLMs and most of those prohibited or discouraged them.
evidence: Highlighting the need for policy, a case study at Purdue University found that prior to formal institutional guidance, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2025.100496 faculty responses to GenAI varied significantly; even in its technology-focused department, less than a third of course syllabi acknowledged LLMs, with most taking prohibitive or discouraging stances (Wiese & Magana, 2024).

unit: AI ethics policy frameworks operate at three interdependent levels: macro-level international and national directives setting normative standards, meso-level institutional governance such as ethics committees adapting frameworks locally, and micro-level operational practices embedding ethics in AI development, audits, and participatory design.
evidence: AI ethics policy frameworks are implemented at three interdependent levels: i) macro-level directives such as international and national/ territory guidelines like the EU's ethics in AI establish overarching normative standards; ii) meso-level institutional mechanisms, involving the creation of ethics committees or governance structures that produce and adapt frameworks locally; and iii) micro-level operational practices, embedding ethics into AI development cycles, audits, and participatory design processes (Barnes & Hutson, 2024; Smuha, 2019; Tirado et al., 2024).

unit: Many universities use tiered GenAI-use frameworks, mostly aimed at assessments, that define permitted, conditional, and unacceptable (misconduct) use; examples include Sydney's two-lane approach, traffic-light systems at Cornell and UCD, and the AI Assessment Scale.
evidence: Many institutions have adopted varying levels of tiered GenAI-use frameworks - dominantly targeting assessments - outlining permitted use, conditional or context-dependent use, and unacceptable use that constitutes misconduct.

unit: The University of Hong Kong moved from default prohibition with permitted use to a decentralised approach in which faculty set course-level GenAI policies, delegating freedom and responsibility to teachers and students.
evidence: The University of Hong Kong (HKU), after a period of permitted use but default prohibition, transitioned to a decentralised approach for faculty members to set their own course-level policies.

unit: HKU's mid-2023 GenAI policy was a flexible framework promoting equitable access, ethical use, and AI literacy and encouraging pedagogical experiments, but lacked prescriptive guidelines and standardised enforcement mechanisms.
evidence: The institutional policy, formulated around mid-2023, offered a flexible framework aimed at promoting equitable access, ethical use, and AI literacy while encouraging pedagogical experiments, but without prescriptive guidelines and clear demarcated or standardised institutional enforcement mechanisms.

unit: The study uses Stephen Ball's concept of policy trajectories to examine how policy and its absence are interpreted, enacted, and creatively resisted by students and teachers, surfacing issues of plagiarism, fairness, overreliance, data privacy, and accessibility.
evidence: Drawing on Stephen Ball's (1993) concept of policy trajectories from the sociology of education, the paper uses this analytical lens to study how policy (and its absence) is discussed, interpreted, implemented/enacted, and creatively resisted by students and teachers, surfacing issues of plagiarism, fairness, overreliance, data privacy, and accessibility.

unit: Participants recommended requiring GenAI usage declarations, dual submissions (AI-assisted plus original work), and oral defences or interviews to complement detection tools in order to address fair use and academic integrity concerns such as authorship, plagiarism, and unfairness between GenAI users and non-users.
evidence: | Fair Use & Academic Integrity       | Authorship, plagiarism, and unfairness between GenAI users and non- users                                          | • Require GenAI usage declarations (e.g., logs) • Promote transparency via dual submissions (AI- assisted þ original) • Complement detection tools with oral defences or interviews                                      |

unit: Students and teachers expressed concern about cognitive decline, loss of motivation, and missed learning opportunities from GenAI overdependence, and recommended balanced use, reflection prompts, and assessments redesigned to discourage full automation.
evidence: | Critical Thinking & Overdependence  | Cognitive decline, loss of motivation, and missed learning opportunities                                           | • Encourage balanced GenAI use • Include reflection prompts • Redesign assessments to discourage full automation, particularly                                                                                           |

unit: For GenAI detection tools, participants worried about false positives creating anxiety and inconsistent penalties, and recommended using detection tools only as preliminary checks and letting students justify flagged usage.
evidence: | Detection & Enforcement             | False positives in GenAI detection tools creating anxiety Inconsistent policies and penalties                      | • Use detection tools as preliminary checks, not final proof • Allow students to justify flagged GenAI usage • Create clear frameworks on permissible GenAI use with examples • Require GenAI usage |

unit: The study analysed interviews in two stages: thematic analysis of ethical concerns and recommendations, then re-analysis through the policy trajectory lens covering interpretive, material, discursive, and enactment dimensions of policy work.
evidence: The analysis proceeded in two stages. First, thematic analysis identified key ethical concerns and recommendations across all interviews. Second, these themes were re-analysed through the policy trajectory lens to understand how they manifest within the interpretive, material, discursive, and enactment dimensions of policy work.

unit: Deductive coding in the study used pre-determined codes based on ethical principles from the literature (transparency, fairness, accountability, privacy) and the policy trajectory framework's key dimensions.
evidence: Deductive coding was undertaken with pre-determined codes based on ethical principles identified in the literature (transparency, fairness, accountability, privacy) and the policy trajectory framework's key dimensions.

unit: In Ball's policy trajectory framework, policy interpretation is the active translation and meaning-making process through which diverse actors make sense of policy texts, which is especially difficult when policies are ambiguous or unclear.
evidence: Within Ball's framework, policy interpretation refers to the active translation and meaning-making processes through which diverse actors make sense of policy texts. This interpretive work is particularly challenging when policies are ambiguous or unclear, as revealed in participants' struggles to understand GenAI guidelines at the programmatic and course level.

unit: Uncertainty about GenAI policy among students produced ambiguity about permissible use, anxiety about inadvertently crossing the line, and perceived unfairness when peers use GenAI without visible enforcement or consequences.
evidence: This uncertainty contributed to interpretational ambiguities around permissible use, anxieties of inadvertently "crossing the line", and the perceived unfairness when peers use it without visible enforcement or consequences.

unit: Students saw inconsistent definitions of acceptable GenAI use, such as grammar assistance being accepted by some teachers but not others, and these inconsistencies occurred within disciplines and programmes rather than only across departments or faculties.
evidence: Generally, students saw inconsistencies in definitions of acceptable versus unacceptable use; for instance, grammar assistance was considered acceptable by some teachers but not by others. These inconsistencies were at the intra-disciplinary and programmatic course level, not simply variances across departments, faculties, or interdisciplinary core curricula.

unit: Students broadly agreed GenAI should be allowed for explanation, summarisation, paraphrasing, research facilitation, grammar checking, ideation and structuring writing, but strongly opposed its use for direct copying, plagiarism, or substantial generation of academic output.
evidence: During the interview, students seemed to come to the consensus that GenAI should be allowed for tasks such as content explanation, summarisation, paraphrasing, research facilitation, and grammar checking, as well as tools for ideation and the structural organisation of writing. However, they strongly opposed its use for direct copying, acts of plagiarism, or substantial generation of academic output.

unit: Many teachers conditionally accepted GenAI for auxiliary functions like grammar refinement or summarisation, but generally opposed it generating significant portions of final output without considerable enhancement or modification.
evidence: Many teachers expressed a conditional acceptance, tolerating or even encouraging the use of GenAI for auxiliary functions like grammar refinement or summarisation (for example, no longer struggling with understanding the quality of writing to focus on their ideas), but usually against the generation of significant portions of the final output without considerable enhancement or modification.

unit: Ambiguous institutional AI policy can foster innovation and hedge uncertainty, but it shifts the interpretive burden onto teachers and students and lets institutions appear progressive while individualising the consequences of GenAI failure.
evidence: While it is essential to acknowledge the value of ambiguous policy positions and organised irresponsibilities (Spector, 2018) in higher educational governance in nurturing innovation and hedging uncertainties, ambiguity shifts the interpretative burden to teachers and students. Critically, ambiguity could strategically allow institutions to be seen as progressive in GenAI adoption, but individualise the consequences of GenAI failure to adopt or comply.

unit: Participants wanted more specific and explicit GenAI guidance, with use cases and examples of acceptable, disclosure-required, and prohibited uses, including both general and discipline-specific guidance.
evidence: Naturally, there was a desire by participants to limit interpretive differences through more specificity and explicit guidance with use cases and examples of what was considered acceptable, required disclosure or prohibited, including general guidance (for example, language support, idea generation/brainstorming) and discipline-specific guidance.

unit: The policy trajectory framework treats policies as perpetually unfolding processes, continuously remade through ongoing negotiations and temporary settlements between competing visions, shaped by reciprocal interactions between external pressures and internal adaptations rather than being fixed texts.
evidence: The policy trajectory framework conceptualises policies as perpetually unfolding processes that undergo constant transformation through reciprocal interactions between external pressures and internal adaptations. Rather than fixed texts, policies are continuously remade through ongoing negotiations and temporary settlements between competing visions.

unit: Although students and teachers at HKU cannot directly change institutional policy documents, their collective struggles to navigate ambiguity actively constitute GenAI policy through lived practice.
evidence: While participants cannot directly alter institutional policy documents and many material constraints, their collective struggles to navigate ambiguity actively constitute policy through lived practice.

unit: Grassroots solutions such as prompt logs, dual submissions and citation guidelines show that AI policy trajectories are actively constructed from below by teachers and students.
evidence: The proliferation of grassroots solutions-prompt logs, dual submissions, citation guidelines-demonstrates policy trajectories being actively constructed from below.

unit: Apparent consensus on transparency, explainability and accountability in AI use masks competing interpretations, such as technical disclosure of GenAI use versus deeper engagement with learning processes, which create multiple and sometimes contradictory policy trajectories within one institution.
evidence: Even apparent consensus around "the culture for transparency, explainability, and accountability" masks competing visions of what these concepts mean in practice. For some, transparency means technical disclosure of GenAI use; for others, it involves deeper engagement with learning processes. These divergent interpretations create multiple, sometimes contradictory policy trajectories operating simultaneously within the same institution.

unit: AI literacy as a standard solution to ethical AI practice becomes contested because teachers hold different assumptions about it, for example knowing how tools work and when they enhance study, or gaining fluency like learning a foreign language through centralised, systematic provision.
evidence: Similarly, the emergence of AI literacy as a standard solution to ethical practice becomes more contested when we drill down into the differences and assumptions of what AI literacy means. Benjamin (Teacher) had a vision of AI-literate teachers as someone "who knows how the tools work … who can basically say this is a way you can use AI to enhance your study. And these are ways that AI won't enhance your studies."

unit: Framing GenAI competence as a digital technical skill may foreclose policy trajectories emphasising critical thinking or creative problem-solving, and equity-based framings may naturalise AI integration as inevitable rather than contestable.
evidence: The framing of GenAI competence as a digital technical skill potentially forecloses other policy trajectories that might emphasise critical thinking or creative problem-solving, showing how specific solutions enable while others constrain future possibilities.

unit: HKU introduced mandatory AI courses for new undergraduates in 2025-2026, comprising a technical introductory course, disciplinary-specific courses and interdisciplinary core courses; its success in balancing critical and ethical engagement with technical proficiency is worth monitoring.
evidence: Incidentally, HKU recently implemented mandatory AI courses for new undergraduates in the 2025-2026 academic year, including an introductory technical AI course taught by the School of Computer and Data Science, disciplinary-specific AI courses offered by the faculties/ departments, and a menu of interdisciplinary AI courses provided as part of the core (general education/liberal arts) curriculum.

unit: Pedagogically sustainable approaches to using AI in education require critical AI literacy, which includes components that go beyond technical proficiency.
evidence: Through my involvement in academic in-service training and workshops focused on GenAI, I have noted a pressing need to develop pedagogically sustainable approaches to AI usage. As many colleagues have pointed out, these approaches require critical AI literacy, which includes several components that go beyond mere technical proficiency.

unit: The author argues that pedagogical sustainability should be a crucial aspect of critical AI literacy.
evidence: One premise of the following text is that a crucial aspect of this literacy should be pedagogical sustainability.

unit: The arts offer particularly useful contexts for developing critical AI literacy because learners can freely experiment with the generative capabilities of the latest models in relatively safe environments, though such experimentation must not come at the cost of recognizing AI's risks.
evidence: Furthermore, it is emphasized here that the arts provide particularly interesting contexts for developing critical AI literacy, as in them, one can experiment freely with the generative capabilities of the latest models in relatively safe environments, concentrating on their creative possibilities. However, such free-form experimentation should not be done at the cost of recognizing the risks of AI use.

unit: Chatbots such as ChatGPT, launched in 2022, made it easy to incorporate GenAI into creative work processes, and the growing availability of multimodal creative GenAI models is making their use ubiquitous.
evidence: While the use of AI is not new in artistic and scientific contexts, chatbots like ChatGPT have made it easy to incorporate GenAI into the creative work processes. With the increasing availability of GenAI models designed to produce creative content in various forms-and across different content modes-one can confidently say that their use is becoming ubiquitous.

unit: Since the 2010s, GenAI has evolved from an experimental technology into a widespread tool in creative industries, bridging art forms and enabling transdisciplinary education and study, which calls for critical dialogue about its potential and limitations.
evidence: Since the 2010s, GenAI has evolved from experimental technology to widespread tool for creative industries, bridging different art forms and providing new possibilities for transdisciplinary education and study. As its influence expands, we need critical dialogue about its potential and limitations.

unit: Large language models are known to hallucinate or 'confabulate', which makes using them for tasks like dream interpretation ironically apt.
evidence: In retrospect, using an LLM for dream interpretation seemed particularly apt, given these models' well-documented tendencies to hallucinate or 'confabulate.'

unit: The AI policy trajectory lifecycle model, built on Ball's policy trajectory framework, shows AI ethics policy as actively negotiated, contested and reformed by multiple actors and contexts rather than implemented top-down and linearly.
evidence: It illustrates how AI ethics policy is not simply implemented top-down and linearly but is actively negotiated, contested, and reformed through the complex interactions of multiple actors and contexts.

unit: In the lifecycle model, the vertical axis is an iterative policy cycle of interpretation, enactment, resistance and evolution, while the horizontal axis captures tension between institutional control with material contexts and individual agency of teachers and students.
evidence: The vertical axis represents the policy trajectory - not as a one-way flow, but as an iterative cycle where policy texts enter the university context and undergo continuous transformation through interpretation, enactment, resistance, and evolution. The horizontal axis captures the ongoing tensions between institutional control (with material contexts) and individual agency or capacities to affect and be affected (teacher discretion, student workaround, creative adaptations), to help think about points at which interventions can happen.

unit: Students and teachers cannot easily change material conditions such as detector accuracy or access to premium AI tools, because material change requires institutional processes, budgets and policy cycles, so they work around constraints instead.
evidence: Hence, individual agency and resistance by students and teachers cannot easily change material conditions (for example, they cannot make Turnitin more accurate, improve access to premium AI tools or institutional infrastructure). Material changes require institutional processes, budgets, and policy cycles. Students and teachers, therefore, need to work around material constraints (using "humanisers", loopholes, or sharing accounts) rather than directly transforming them.

unit: Acts of resistance by students can immediately challenge dominant discourses, such as students distancing themselves from GenAI after recognising its limitations, which counters the 'AI efficiency' narrative.
evidence: However, acts of resistance can immediately challenge dominant narratives. For example, the distancing from GenAI by the students after realising its limitations (enactment) can directly counter the "AI efficiency" narrative (discourse).

unit: Students' and teachers' confusion about university GenAI policy shows a desire for centralised university-wide guidance setting clear baselines for acceptable GenAI use.
evidence: For university leaders and policymakers, policy ambiguities - illustrated by the lack of clarity among students and teachers about the university's GenAI policy and the widespread confusion and opacity regarding what constitutes acceptable - show a desire from students and teachers for centralised university-wide guidance to establish clear baselines for acceptable GenAI use, reinforcing recommendations by Johnston et al. (2024).

unit: Policies that only shift discursive constructions without addressing material and structural contexts such as assessment redesign risk creating 'illusions of assessment security'.
evidence: Moreover, Corbin et al. (2025) warn against creating policies that establish "illusions of assessment security" - working on shifting discursive constructions without attending to the underlying material and structural contexts, such as assessment redesign.

unit: Traditional education policy cycles measured in semesters and years are mismatched with rapid GenAI development, so universities need adaptive 'liquid policymaking' with participatory input from students and teachers, such as iterative cycles, feedback loops, pilots and sandboxes.
evidence: This policy lag signals the need to develop new mechanisms of liquid policymaking that can adapt progressively, with ongoing participatory input from students and teachers to anticipate enactment trajectories. This could mean shorter-term iterative policy cycles, dynamic policy manuals, real-time feedback loops, continual pilots and within courses and programmes, sandbox environments, activating student/teacher partnership expertise, clear institutional communication channels, and developing cross-institutional consortia for shared policy learning.

unit: GenAI policy should be locally situated and use non-binding guidelines with a baseline, distinguishing productive emulation from passive copying and using graduated consequences rather than zero tolerance, since neither bans nor appeals to conscience have worked.
evidence: Given these contextual factors, non-binding guidelines alongside a baseline can allow for flexibility to address (inter)disciplinary or course-specific needs as the technology and learning environment evolve. Such guidelines could distinguish between productive emulation (using GenAI to learn from model responses) versus passive copying (submitting generated text without engagement) and include graduated consequences rather than zero-tolerance approaches. Neither banning students from use nor simply appealing to their good conscience has proven effective.

unit: GenAI refers to self-adaptive digital technologies that use artificial intelligence for creative purposes, emulating human intelligence; as of Fall 2024 they were epitomized by multimodal large language models able to generate content in various formats.
evidence: GenAI refers to self-adaptive digital technologies that harness artificial intelligence (AI) for creative purposes, emulating human intelligence. As of Fall 2024, when this introduction was written, such technologies were epitomized by multimodal large language models (MLLMs) capable of generating content across various formats.

unit: Some experts argue that multimodal generative models may make it virtually impossible to distinguish human-made from machine-made output, forcing a reconsideration of the role of machines in creative domains.
evidence: Some experts argue that the development of such models may make it virtually impossible to differentiate between human and machine-made output, forcing us to reconsider the role of machines in creative domains (see, e.g., Danesi 2024; Miller 2019).

unit: The rapid advancement of GenAI may blur the line between AI-produced content that represents reality and content that merely presents, leaving it questionable whether GenAI is an epistemic agent judged by how it represents reality.
evidence: Moreover, the rapid advancement of GenAI may blur the line between AI-produced content that represents and that which merely presents. The question of whether GenAI is an epistemic agent that can be judged on account of how it represents reality remains questionable.

unit: Some critics, such as Bender et al. (2021), regard GenAI as a 'stochastic parrot' that only statistically predicts desired content.
evidence: Some critics regard GenAI as a mere 'stochastic parrot' capable only of statistically predicting desired content (Bender et al. 2021).

unit: Viewing GenAI merely as a statistical prediction mechanism overlooks its hallucinating or 'confabulating' ability to generate new content by filling in gaps, which sometimes yields surprising results.
evidence: However, taking GenAI merely as a statistic prediction mechanism overlooks its hallucinating or 'confabulating' abilities-its capacity to generate new content by filling in gaps, which sometimes produces surprising results (Ramsøy 2024; Sui et al. 2024).

unit: In this context, 'transformation' and 'transformative' refer to education's capacity to foster human growth and Bildung, both by changing learners and by altering the conditions of their agency.
evidence: The noun 'transformation' and the adjective 'transformative' in this context refer to education's capacity to foster human growth and Bildung, not only by changing those who are educated but also by altering the conditions of their agency.

unit: Educational transformation does not necessarily mean an overhaul of a learner's prior disposition; it is often subtle, such as developing new ways of seeing, hearing, and listening.
evidence: This does not necessarily imply an overhaul of one's previous disposition-though that can occur. Often, the changes are subtle, such as developing new ways of seeing, hearing, and listening.

unit: Following Jacques Rancière, art can transform subtly and may even be transgressive because it can refashion the 'distribution of the sensible', meaning our sensory encounter with the world and how we share it as aesthetically meaningful.
evidence: As Jacques Rancière (2004) argues, it can even be considered transgressive on account of its capability to refashion the 'distribution of the sensible'-our sensory encounter with the world and how we share it as aesthetically meaningful.

unit: In art(s) education, GenAI, like all technologies, should be evaluated by its ability to transform our relationships with the world and with each other.
evidence: For now, it is crucial to note that GenAI, like all technologies, should be evaluated in art(s) education based on its ability to transform our relationships with the world and each other.

unit: Praxis is a critical and self-reflective way of doing things together: a form of social action that constantly observes its conditions and stays alert to the need for adjustment.
evidence: 'Praxis' in this context refers to a critical and self-reflective way of doing things together. It is a form of social action that is able to constantly observe its conditions, remaining alert to the potential need for adjustment.

unit: The book treats praxis as an inherently reflective and critical practice aimed at the best outcomes for the people involved, so praxis always carries an ethical element.
evidence: While praxis has been discussed in various ways in philosophical and educational literature (see, e.g., Arendt 1989; Carr and Kemmis 1986; Freire 1985; Grundy 1987; Kemmis and Smith 2008), this book views it as an inherently reflective and critical practice that aims for the best outcomes for the persons involved. Thus, praxis always implicates an ethical element.

evidence: Aligning with critical studies of technology, this book considers GenAI as a catalyst for transforming technologically mediated praxes rather than simply a set of technical solutions confined within existing value frameworks. unit: The book adopts a pragmatic yet critical stance balancing technological optimism and skepticism, aiming for an inclusive, ethically alert exploration of GenAI's transformative potential in art(s) education while watching for adverse effects.

Such an approach seeks to facilitate a dynamic, inclusive, and ethically alert exploration of GenAI's transformative potential in art(s) education within late modernity while remaining alert to its possible adverse effects.

unit: The chapter uses sustainability as an umbrella concept covering ecological, social, cultural, political, economic, and technological dimensions, together with aesthetic and pedagogical ones, in order to frame sustainable AI art(s) pedagogies responding to GenAI's expanding creative possibilities.
evidence: This chapter makes a case for developing sustainable AI art(s) pedagogies in response to GenAI's rapidly expanding creative possibilities. Here, sustainability provides an umbrella concept encompassing ecological, social, cultural, political, economic, and technological dimensions-along with aesthetic and pedagogical ones.

unit: The chapter treats art(s) education as a transdisciplinary domain, focusing mainly on sonic and visual arts, so that connections across artistic disciplines can serve as a foundation for sustainable AI art(s) pedagogies.
evidence: Art(s) education is here understood as a transdisciplinary domain, though the focus of the chapter again remains primarily on sonic and visual arts. A broad definition of art(s) education hopefully helps readers discover meaningful connections between these and other artistic disciplines while recognizing their distinct characteristics. These connections can serve as a foundation for developing sustainable AI art(s) pedagogies.

unit: Because of its performative nature, GenAI offers an interesting case for reconsidering human-machine co-creation, which is at the heart of sustainable AI art(s) pedagogies.
evidence: Through its performative nature, GenAI provides an interesting case for reconsidering human-machine co-creation at the heart of such pedagogies.

unit: Pedagogical sustainability is proposed as a framework for understanding how different sustainability dimensions can help prepare future generations to identify global challenges and possibly develop solutions to them.
evidence: It is suggested here that pedagogical sustainability provides a valuable framework for understanding how various sustainability dimensions can help prepare future generations to identify global challenges and, maybe, also to develop solutions to these challenges.

unit: Sustainability has several dimensions: political sustainability concerns collective decision-making and advocacy, economic sustainability concerns the limits of value creation and exchange, technological sustainability concerns the development and use of tools and infrastructure, and aesthetic sustainability concerns how we perceive our living environments.
evidence: Political sustainability examines collective decision-making and advocacy (Heinrichs and Biermann 2016). Economic sustainability encompasses the limits of value creation and exchange (Jeronen 2020). Technological sustainability addresses the development and use of tools and infrastructure (Vacchi et al. 2021). Aesthetic sustainability considers how we perceive our living environments (Allen 2019).
section_path: GenAI and Art(s) Education for Sustainability

unit: The authors develop pedagogical sustainability on the idea that education can both aim for sustainability and be sustainable in itself, going beyond earlier uses of the term as a synonym for sustainability education.
evidence: While the concept of pedagogical sustainability has been used before in educational literature (see e.g., Sharma 2023) to characterize "the development of values, attitudes, and behaviors that promote long-term well-being for both individuals and the planet" (ibid., 13), or simply as a synonym for sustainability education, here the concept is developed based on the idea that education can both aim for sustainability and be sustainable in itself.
section_path: GenAI and Art(s) Education for Sustainability

unit: Different sustainability goals can conflict, as historical cases show economic, social, or cultural sustainability clashing with ecological sustainability.
evidence: For instance, historical evidence shows cases where economic, social, or cultural sustainability has conflicted with ecological sustainability (see, e.g., Duany et al. 2001; Mekonnen et al. 2022; Souza-Rodrigues 2019).

unit: Artists and art educators maintain that art can promote sustainability by stimulating behavioral change and engaging communities in thinking about environmental challenges.
evidence: Whatever the case, artists and art(s) educators have long maintained that art can offer pathways to sustainability by stimulating behavioral change and engaging communities in thinking about environmental challenges (see, e.g., Clarke and Hulbert 2016; Foster et al. 2019; Illeris 2012; Inwood and Taylor 2012; Mantoan 2021; Pavlou 2024).
section_path: GenAI and Art(s) Education for Sustainability

unit: The arts may allow exploration of sustainability in ways other disciplines cannot; for example, posthumanist perspectives on systemic entanglements may be better grasped through artistic imagination.
evidence: In line with the latter view, it can be further argued that the arts enable us to explore questions of sustainability in ways other disciplines cannot. For example, it can be claimed that posthumanist perspectives on systemic entanglements may be better understood through artistic imagination than through other forms of knowledge (Bentz et al. 2022).
